docs.title: SharedHousehold Docs & Reports
docs.text:
The public site for SharedHousehold documentation, decisions, and agent reports.

  • Source of truth: the private repository share-org/share (docs/)
  • Site: this site is built with MkDocs Material and published automatically from the repository's docs/ directory.

  • BR-001 — Agent permission architecture
  • ADR-001 — Agent permission restrictions

docs.title: Republishing
docs.text: The site republishes automatically when docs change on main. To force a republish, run the docs-publish workflow from the Actions tab of share-org/share (see docs/development/docs-publishing.md).

docs.title: Flow
docs.text:
Human
  -> GitHub issue
  -> [brainstorming when a design decision exists]
  -> product-planner
  -> architect
  -> implementation agent (backend and/or frontend)
  -> qa-engineer
  -> code-reviewer
  -> security-reviewer (when relevant)
  -> Human review
  -> Merge

The orchestrator decides whether brainstorming is needed before planning. See docs/ai/brainstorms/ for decision reports and the brainstorming skill.

docs.title: Default workflow (minimum set required)
docs.text:
Issue
  -> [brainstorming when a design decision exists]
  -> product-planner
  -> architect
  -> implementation agent
  -> qa-engineer
  -> code-reviewer
  -> security-reviewer (when relevant)
  -> human review
  • Use documentation only when documentation actually changes.
  • Use researcher only for external/technical research tasks.
  • Do not fire every agent on every task. The orchestrator selects the minimum set and stops unnecessary chains.

docs.title: Orchestrator behavior
docs.text:
• Prefer "one strong planning call + one implementation agent + one QA/review loop" over spawning many redundant agents.
  • The orchestrator never implements directly.
  • The orchestrator detects design decisions and delegates those to the brainstormer instead of deciding alone.

docs.title: Collaborative brainstorming
docs.text:
• Runs as independent proposals -> cross-critique -> synthesis among only the relevant specialists (2-4), then selects a solution autonomously.
  • Durable report written to docs/ai/brainstorms/BR-NNN-<topic>.md; long-term decisions recorded as ADRs.
  • Agents are autonomous by default: analyze, discuss, decide, report, implement. The user receives the decision as a report and can override later.
  • Never stop simply because several solutions exist. Block only when the task is genuinely unsafe, impossible, or contradictory (BLOCKED report).

docs.title: Nesting note
docs.text: The standard workflow keeps subagent delegation to one level, but the brainstorming phase intentionally runs one extra level (orchestrator -> brainstormer -> specialists) as designed.

docs.title: Cheap/free model rules
docs.text:
The system is intentionally optimized for low-cost models.

  1. Give agents one task at a time.
  2. Keep prompts short and repository rules centralized in AGENTS.md.
  3. Load documents lazily.
  4. Prefer deterministic checklists.
  5. Use specialized read-only reviewers instead of asking one model to reason about everything.
  6. Limit subagent nesting to one level.
  7. Avoid repeated whole-repository scans.
  8. Ask the model to inspect relevant files first.
  9. Use automated tests as the main correctness feedback mechanism.
  10. Make the model produce structured output.
  11. Never rely on hidden conversation memory for critical architecture decisions.
  12. Put durable knowledge into the repository.

docs.title: Agent budget policy
docs.text:
For a small task:

Implementation only

For a normal feature:

Product-planner -> Architect -> Implementer -> Reviewer

For a high-risk feature:

Brainstorming (when a design decision exists)
  -> Product-planner -> Architect -> Implementer -> Reviewer -> QA

(Add security-reviewer when authentication/authorization, household data, financial logic, or external integrations are involved.)

Do not launch all agents for every trivial change.

docs.title: Fallback policy
docs.text: See docs/ai/model-strategy.md. Fallbacks are optional and depend on the configured providers. After two materially similar failures, escalate or change strategy instead of blindly retrying.

docs.title: Agent Workflow — reading the repository from GitHub
docs.text: This document explains how the SharedHousehold agent team operates and how a human owner runs the project from GitHub Issues and Pull Requests, with OpenCode executing behind the scenes in GitHub Actions.

docs.title: The pipeline at a glance
docs.text:
Human (GitHub)
   │  creates / edits / comments an Issue
   ▼
GitHub Event / orchestration workflow
   │  (opencode-command.yml, opencode-issue-triage.yml, opencode-pr-review.yml,
   │   opencode-agent-status.yml)
   ▼
OpenCode Orchestrator (primary agent, runs in a GitHub Actions runner)
   │  task tool → product-planner / brainstormer / architect / implementers /
   │              qa / reviewers / security / documentation / researcher
   ▼
Implementation → branch → commits → Pull Request
   ▼
QA → Code review (→ security review when relevant)
   ▼
Human approval (default gate) → merge → CI (ci.yml) → done

A second entry point feeds the same engine: the prototype feedback loop (maquette annotation layer → prototype-feedback issue → brainstorm panel → sub-issues → parallel chains). See "Prototype feedback loop" below.

In autopilot mode (AUTOPILOT == 'on'), issues opened by trusted actors skip the per-phase /oc commands: opencode-pipeline.yml drives analyze → implement → qa → review and self-dispatches the next phase. The human merge gate, status:blocked halting, and /oc stop|continue overrides all still apply. See docs/ai/github-agent-commands.md.

GitHub is the system of record. The repository is the system of knowledge (docs/, decisions, code). OpenCode is the execution engine and is deliberately transient — a new OpenCode process reconstructs state by reading GitHub and the repository.

docs.title: How an Issue moves through the system
1. Issue created → triage
docs.text:
opencode-issue-triage.yml runs on issues: opened. The orchestrator:

  1. reads the issue and relevant docs,
  2. decides whether a design decision is required,
  3. brainstorms if needed (writes docs/ai/brainstorms/BR-NNN-*.md, posts a concise summary on the Issue),
  4. marks the Issue status:ready (or status:discovery + open questions).

Implementation is never started automatically. It requires an explicit /oc implement from a trusted human.

docs.title: 2. Command
docs.text: A human comments /oc <command> (optionally /oc @agent <command>). The opencode-command.yml workflow validates the actor, assigns a run ID, posts a start/complete status on the Issue, and runs OpenCode.

docs.title: 3. Implementation
docs.text: /oc implement → the orchestrator selects the implementation agent, creates a branch (feature/EXP-105-* or agent/<topic>-<agent>), commits with Git trailers (Agent, Agent-Run, Issue), opens a PR, and posts the PR link. When needed, /oc plan runs first: it writes docs/ai/plans/PLAN-*.md on a plan/<issue>-* branch and opens a PR that /oc implement then executes. Human approval remains the default merge gate.

docs.title: 4. QA and review
docs.text:
• opencode-pr-review.yml runs a read-only review automatically for human-authored PRs (skips bot-authored PRs to prevent self-review).
  • opencode-pr-review.yml and /oc qa / /oc review run the QA and review agents, which post PASS/FAIL evidence on the PR/Issue.

docs.title: 5. Human approval
docs.text: The human reviews the PR in GitHub, asks for fixes via comments or /oc, and merges. CI (ci.yml, mvn verify) runs on every push/PR.

docs.title: Status (the issue state machine)
docs.text:
BACKLOG → DISCOVERY → READY → IN_PROGRESS → REVIEW → QA → DONE
                                ↘ BLOCKED
Label Meaning Applied when status:backlog created, not started created status:discovery analyzing/brainstorming/planning triage, /oc analyze, /oc brainstorm, /oc plan, /oc decide status:ready specified, implementation can start triage completes with a sufficient spec status:in-progress implementation running /oc implement status:review pending code review /oc review, automatic PR review status:qa waiting for QA verification /oc qa status:blocked waiting on a human or external dependency /oc stop, a BLOCKED report status:done complete and merged merged

docs.title: Type
docs.text: type:feature, type:bug, type:architecture, type:technical-debt, type:brainstorm.

docs.title: Priority
docs.text: priority:p0 (blocker) … priority:p3 (lowest).

docs.title: Agent (logical identity)
docs.text: agent:orchestrator, agent:product, agent:architect, agent:backend, agent:frontend, agent:qa, agent:security, agent:review, agent:documentation. These record which logical agent is/was active — there is one automation identity, not fake per-agent users.

docs.title: Prototype feedback
docs.text:
Label Meaning Applied when prototype-feedback filed from the published maquette's annotation layer by the human, through the prefilled issue URL feedback:parent a feedback issue already fanned out into sub-issues by the intake run feedback:child sub-issue derived from a parent feedback issue by the intake run feedback:child-of-<issue> the parent link, one label per sub-issue by the intake run (generated, not in setup-labels.sh)

feedback:child-of-<issue> is what lets the pipeline close a parent without ever editing an issue body: after a merge it lists the parent's children and closes the parent only when none are open.

docs.title: Prototype feedback loop
docs.text:
maquette (?annotate=1)  ->  click a component  ->  issue labeled prototype-feedback
   ->  opencode-prototype-feedback.yml
        ->  brainstorm panel: designer (UX), product, architect, backend, QA
        ->  synthesis: BR report + one plan per track
        ->  sub-issues UX / FRONTEND / BACKEND, label feedback:child-of-<parent>
   ->  opencode-pipeline.yml, one parallel chain per sub-issue
   ->  parent feedback issue closes when every child is merged
Stage Actor What happens Capture human static annotation layer in the maquette; pre-fills screen, data-uid, CSS path, prototype URL, viewport Intake brainstormer (delegated by orchestrator) panel discussion → BR-NNN-*.md (+ ADR when durable) Decomposition orchestrator one sub-issue + one PLAN-*.md per affected track; UX → designer, FRONTEND → frontend-implementer, BACKEND → backend-implementer Execution per sub-issue the normal implement → qa → review → auto-merge chain, in parallel Completion opencode-pipeline.yml parent closed automatically when no child is open

Properties worth knowing:

  • Trust gate. The prototype is public, so only a prototype-feedback issue whose author is in OC_TRUSTED_ACTORS is executed. Anything else is parked as status:backlog with an explanatory comment. The issue body is untrusted input: the intake reads it through the gh JSON API and never interpolates it into a shell command (AGENTS.md, security rules).
  • No double handling. opencode-issue-triage.yml skips issues carrying prototype-feedback; the intake skips issues already carrying feedback:parent. Both gates are label-driven, so the loop cannot re-trigger.
  • No design ceremony for nits. The intake is told to skip the panel and close the parent directly when the feedback is a copy/colour/label tweak.
  • The pre-fill records the element data-uid, so a new annotatable component needs a data-uid on its structural element. See docs/product/maquette/maquette.md.

docs.title: Status markers
docs.text:
Meaningful state changes are posted as standardized comments:

🤖 STARTED | 🤖 ANALYZING | 🤖 BRAINSTORMING | 🤖 PLANNING | 🤖 IMPLEMENTING
🤖 TESTING | 🤖 REVIEWING | 🤖 BLOCKED | 🤖 COMPLETED

These are concise; durable analysis lives in docs/ai/brainstorms/ and PRs.

docs.title: Run IDs and identity
docs.text:
Every execution has a run ID: run-YYYY-MM-DD-NNNN.

Where to find a run ID:

  • in the status comments on the Issue/PR,
  • in Git trailers on agent commits,
  • in the PR's AI Execution table,
  • in brainstorm/decision reports,
  • in workflow logs.

The run ID ties a human request → Issue → agent → model → branch → commits → PR → QA/review → merge. See the audit chain below.

docs.title: The audit chain (traceability)
docs.text:
For any task you should be able to answer:

Question Where to look Who requested it? the issue creator / command comment author (github.actor) Which Issue? Issue: #N trailers, Closes #N Which agent? Agent: <name> trailers/comments, agent:* labels Which run? Agent-Run: run-… trailers, status comments Which model? the AI Execution table on the PR + .github/oc-models.json Which decision? docs/ai/brainstorms/BR-NNN-*.md + ADRs Which files changed? the PR diff Which branch / commits? the PR Which tests? CI run + QA comment evidence Which reviewers? review comments + status:review Who approved/meged? the PR "merged by" info

Chain shape:

Human → Issue #N → Run ID → Brainstorm report → ADR → Branch → Commit(s)
      → PR → QA result → Security result → Human approval → Merge

docs.title: GitHub Project (fields)
docs.text:
A GitHub Project v2 can hold status automation. Recommended fields:

Status, Type, Priority, Domain, Agent, Current Run, Milestone, Risk, AI Decision.

Automating these fields requires a token that can write the Project (project scope for classic PAT, or a fine-grained token with "Projects" read/write) and org/owner setup — that is intentionally NOT embedded in the workflows or the repo (no credentials in the repository). Set it up manually and connect the Status field to the status:* labels if you want Board integration.

docs.title: Human overrides
docs.text:
An explicit human comment always overrides an earlier agent decision. Example:

Agent: I selected option B.
Human: /oc use option A instead

The orchestrator records the override, explains impact, updates the plan, and continues with option A.

docs.title: Loop protection
docs.text: Workflows ignore comments/issues authored by bot actors (*[bot]). Moving the state forward is always the human's action; agent comments cannot re-trigger themselves. PRs created by the agent team use GITHUB_TOKEN, so they do not spur new auto-review runs — review is requested explicitly or runs once for human-authored PRs.

docs.title: Recovery
docs.text: If a workflow fails, a model times out, or a partial implementation exists, recover by running opencode-agent-status from the Actions tab (or comment /oc status): the orchestrator inspects existing branches, PRs, comments, run metadata, and CI, then reports current state and the recommended next action instead of duplicating work.

docs.title: Required / recommended GitHub setup
docs.text:
• Labels: bash scripts/setup-labels.sh (upsert the standardized label set).
  • Repository variable OC_TRUSTED_ACTORS: CSV of human accounts allowed to run mutation commands, e.g. oussAbd.
  • Secrets (all optional): OPENCODE_API_KEY (OpenCode gateway/team key), provider keys (e.g. ANTHROPIC_API_KEY) if models move off the free gateway.
  • GitHub Project v2 fields: see above (manual).
  • Branch protection on main (requires a paid plan; convention-only otherwise: agents never merge).

docs.title: Autonomy Budget
docs.text:
Hard limits that keep autonomous execution bounded. The manager must stop gracefully when a limit is reached — never exceed a budget to "finish" something.

Limits are repository variables, so they can be tuned without a code change. A missing or empty variable means "use the default below", never "unlimited".

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
Variable Default Meaning MANAGER_MAX_NEW_ISSUES_PER_CYCLE 3 New feature issues created in one heartbeat. MANAGER_MAX_PRS_IN_FLIGHT 3 Open implementation PRs before the manager stops creating new work. MANAGER_MAX_CONCURRENT_AGENTS 2 Specialists the manager may have in flight at once. MANAGER_MAX_RETRIES_SAME_STRATEGY 2 Attempts with the same approach before reassessing. MANAGER_MAX_AUTONOMOUS_ATTEMPTS 3 Total attempts on one issue before it becomes status:blocked. MANAGER_MAX_CYCLES_PER_HOUR 4 Reconciliation cycles started in an hour. MANAGER_HEARTBEAT_MINUTES 30 Heartbeat interval, clamped to a floor of 15. Not applied to an explicit workflow_dispatch.

Per the request that this system came from, "24/7" means continuously monitor and reconcile, not continuously create tasks. The issue cap is the main guardrail against that misreading.

docs.title: How the heartbeat interval is enforced
docs.text:
GitHub Actions cron cannot read repository variables, so the schedule is fixed at 15 minutes in .github/workflows/project-manager-loop.yml and MANAGER_HEARTBEAT_MINUTES is applied at run time: the gate measures how long since the Manager Ledger was last updated and skips the cycle if it is inside the interval, clamped to a 15-minute floor.

So the schedule is the cadence and the variable is the rate limit. Raising MANAGER_HEARTBEAT_MINUTES above 15 works immediately; lowering it below 15 does not, because the floor is deliberate. Changing the cadence itself means editing the workflow, which is a guardrail path and therefore always a human merge.

Set the variable to 15 to match the cron. With the default of 30 the two disagree: cron fires every 15 minutes, and every second tick is skipped by the gate as rate-limited. The result looks like a healthy loop on the Actions tab — a run every 15 minutes, green — while the manager actually acts every 30. The skipped run is reported, not silent, but a green run that deliberately did nothing is easy to mistake for progress. MANAGER_HEARTBEAT_MINUTES=15 removes the gap without touching the workflow.

docs.title: An explicit dispatch is never throttled
docs.text:
The interval applies to every trigger except workflow_dispatch. The rate limit exists to damp triggers that fire on their own — a CI completion, a label change, the clock — each of which can happen several times between two heartbeats. A dispatch is the opposite: a person pressed "run", by hand, on purpose.

Throttling a request makes the loop untestable. Every fix needs a live cycle to prove itself, and if the human is the thing being throttled there is no way to get one without first waiting out the interval. So to test a change, dispatch the workflow and it runs now:

/oc manager run

or Actions → project-manager → Run workflow on main.

The bypass is announced as a ::notice in the run and recorded in the Manager Ledger next to the result, so a cycle that overrode the throttle is always distinguishable from one that waited its turn.

It skips the throttle and nothing else. The manager:paused emergency stop and MANAGER_AUTONOMY=human_only are evaluated before the interval and still apply to a dispatch. A cycle started by hand is still a gated cycle.

MANAGER_MAX_CYCLES_PER_HOUR is not a shell limit — it is the manager's own bookkeeping — so repeated manual dispatches are not hard-capped. The oc-project-manager concurrency group still serialises them: a second cycle queues behind the first rather than running beside it.

docs.title: Which limits are enforced where
docs.text:
Limit Enforced by MANAGER_HEARTBEAT_MINUTES shell gate (deterministic), except an explicit workflow_dispatch MANAGER_MAX_NEW_ISSUES_PER_CYCLE manager, against the ledger MANAGER_MAX_PRS_IN_FLIGHT manager, before creating work MANAGER_MAX_CONCURRENT_AGENTS manager, when delegating MANAGER_MAX_RETRIES_SAME_STRATEGY manager, from the ledger MANAGER_MAX_AUTONOMOUS_ATTEMPTS manager, from the ledger

Only the stop conditions and the heartbeat interval are enforced in shell, because only those must hold even if the model misbehaves. The counting limits are the manager's own bookkeeping, exported into its environment as variables so it reads one source of truth instead of remembering numbers.

docs.title: What happens when a budget is reached
docs.text:
1. Stop starting new work immediately.
  2. Record the remaining work in the ledger as queued for the next cycle, with the reason it was deferred.
  3. Report it in the cycle's output under ## Budget used.
  4. Do not retry the same action later in the same cycle.

Exceeding a budget to finish something is a defect, not initiative.

docs.title: Failure and retry budget
docs.text:
• Same strategy, maximum 2 attempts. After that, change something real: a different model, a different agent, a smaller task, or a split task.
  • Maximum 3 autonomous attempts per issue. On exhaustion, mark the issue status:blocked with evidence — what was tried, what failed, what is needed — and stop.
  • Never retry a status:blocked issue without an explicit human /oc continue.
  • Retries are counted in the ledger so the count survives a restart.

docs.title: Why these limits exist
docs.text: The failure mode being designed against is a runaway autonomous loop: an agent creates work, its own output triggers it, and the system generates work faster than it can converge. Recursion guards and idempotency checks reduce that risk, but a numeric ceiling is the only thing that actually bounds it. If the caps are routinely hit, the right response is to retune them or fix the sequencing — not to raise them reflexively.

docs.title: Autonomy Policy
docs.text:
How much the Project Manager may do without asking the founder. This document is the normative reference; the agent prompt implements it and scripts/test-project-manager.sh pins its safety clauses.

The founder is always the product authority and always the safety boundary. No autonomy level permits the manager to redefine the business vision, reach production, or merge a guardrail change.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
Autonomy is a repository variable, not a code change:

MANAGER_AUTONOMY = human_only | supervised | autonomous

Default: supervised.

It is deliberately independent of the existing AUTOPILOT variable, which governs the pre-existing pipeline. The two must not be conflated: AUTOPILOT=on means "trusted issues flow through the pipeline automatically". It does not grant the manager merge authority. Raising the manager's power is a separate, explicit act.

To change it:

gh variable set MANAGER_AUTONOMY --body autonomous

docs.title: human_only
docs.text: Analyse and propose. Create no issues, change no labels, delegate no agents, merge nothing. Useful for auditing what the manager would do before letting it act.

docs.title: supervised — default
docs.text:
Run the full delivery loop: reconcile, create issues, delegate specialists, drive the pipeline through QA and review, open PRs, maintain the ledger and roadmap status.

Stops before merging. Implementation PRs are left for the founder to merge.

This is the recommended steady state. It captures most of the value — sequencing, proactive work, unblocking, stalled-PR detection — while keeping the single highest-risk action (an ungated merge) human.

docs.title: autonomous
docs.text:
Everything in supervised, plus merging implementation PRs when every gate in the merge policy passes.

Two carve-outs are permanent and apply at every level, including autonomous:

  • Guardrail changes are never merged by the manager. Any PR touching .github/, .opencode/, AGENTS.md or oc-models.json is merged by the founder by hand.
  • CRITICAL risk (risk:critical) is propose-only. Never implemented, never merged.

A third prohibition is not a carve-out but an invariant of the merge path: the manager never uses --admin, never bypasses branch protection, and never force-pushes main. If branch protection refuses a merge, that refusal is correct behaviour — the manager stops and escalates.

docs.title: Operating states
docs.text:
Separate from the mode, and checked at the start of every run:

State Behaviour NORMAL Proceed per the configured mode. PAUSED Set by the manager:paused label on any open issue. Analyse state and report it. Start no new work. EMERGENCY_STOP MANAGER_AUTONOMY=human_only. Start nothing at all. Report and exit.

A stop signal that still starts work is not a stop signal. PAUSED and EMERGENCY_STOP must produce zero new issues, zero new delegations and zero merges.

docs.title: Risk classes
docs.text:
Every change is classified before implementation is delegated. The class decides the gates.

Class Typical changes Handling LOW documentation, copy, a simple UI adjustment, an isolated test, a safe refactor may proceed autonomously in any mode MEDIUM an ordinary application feature, an additive API change, a database migration with a tested rollback proceeds automatically through the normal QA + review gates HIGH authentication, authorization, payment or money logic, a major migration, an architecture change, a data migration, an external integration requires an explicit security-reviewer pass, and is never auto-merged without one CRITICAL production infrastructure, a destructive migration, a security-boundary change, secrets, production data modification propose only. Never implement, never merge. Escalate to the founder with status:blocked and evidence.

Classification is not a formality. "We only changed a query" is how a money bug gets shipped. When genuinely unsure between two classes, take the higher one.

docs.title: Financial domain
docs.text:
This application handles money. The following are HIGH or above by default:

currency   rounding   allocations   balances   settlements   transaction history

Additional standing rules for the manager:

  • Never allow a test, validation, invariant or rounding rule around a financial calculation to be weakened, skipped, deleted, or marked tolerated in order to make something pass.
  • Never accept "close enough" arithmetic. Exact decimal arithmetic with explicit scale and explicit, tested rounding is the standard; double or float for money is never acceptable.
  • If a money change cannot be made correct, that is a status:blocked with evidence — not a shippable approximation.

docs.title: What always requires the founder
docs.text:
Regardless of mode:

  • changing the product vision, MVP scope or business model
  • removing a major feature
  • a destructive data operation
  • a production security-boundary change
  • an irreversible architecture decision
  • a decision with significant infrastructure cost
  • any production access of any kind

docs.title: Human override
docs.text:
A human comment always beats an earlier manager decision. On override the manager must record the decision, stop conflicting work, update the issue, plan and roadmap status, and continue with the founder's choice. It must not re-litigate the point in a later cycle.

See docs/architecture/decisions/ADR-002-autonomous-project-manager.md for the rationale, and in particular for the recorded decision that the manager merges directly rather than delegating to the pipeline.

docs.title: Context management
docs.text: Use a layered context strategy. Agents must not dump the entire repository into context.

docs.title: Layer 1: Always available
docs.text:
AGENTS.md
current issue

docs.title: Layer 2: Load only when needed
docs.text:
domain-model.md
architecture.md
security.md
relevant ADRs
relevant source files

docs.title: Layer 3: Task-specific
docs.text:
specific module
specific tests
specific migration
specific API contract

For a feature change, the preferred order is:

Issue
 -> AGENTS.md
 -> relevant docs
 -> affected code
 -> tests
 -> implementation
 -> targeted verification

docs.title: Context-efficiency rules
docs.text:
• Never read the entire repository unless necessary.
  • Start with the issue and affected files.
  • Search before reading large files.
  • Read only relevant sections.
  • Prefer existing implementations/patterns.
  • Do not repeat information already present in repository documentation.
  • Do not include entire source files in prompts or reports.
  • Keep intermediate outputs concise.
  • Do not call multiple agents when one agent can solve the task.
  • Do not repeatedly retry the same failed approach.
  • Use targeted tests before the complete suite.
  • After two materially similar failures, escalate or change strategy.

These rules are also recorded in AGENTS.md and embedded in agent prompts.

docs.title: Brainstorming context strategy
docs.text:
For a brainstorming session, give each participant minimal independent context, never the whole repository:

Problem
+ relevant documentation
+ small set of relevant files
+ specific question

Do not send:

entire repository
+ entire architecture
+ all documentation
  • Independent proposals receive minimal context; only the synthesis step combines the relevant proposals.
  • Default: 2-4 specialist agents + one synthesis pass. For very simple design questions, 2 agents + synthesis is sufficient.
  • Limit discussion to 3 rounds (proposals, cross-critique, synthesis) maximum.

docs.title: GitHub Agent Commands
docs.text: The human owner drives the agent team from GitHub. Comment on an Issue or PR with a command starting with /oc (the /opencode alias also works). OpenCode runs inside GitHub Actions using the repository's configured agents and models.

docs.title: Command list
docs.text: Command Group What it does Changes code? /oc analyze <topic> analysis Reads the issue/thread and posts an analysis no /oc brainstorm <topic> planning Runs collaborative brainstorming, writes docs/ai/brainstorms/BR-NNN-*.md, posts a summary comment writes reports /oc plan <feature> planning Writes docs/ai/plans/PLAN-*.md, opens a plan PR no /oc implement implementation Verifies readiness, creates a branch, implements, tests, opens/updates a PR yes /oc review review Independent code review of the current change/PR no /oc qa [criteria] QA Verifies acceptance criteria with test evidence (PASS/FAIL/BLOCKED) no (tests only) /oc decide <options> decision Evaluates alternatives and records a decision writes decisions /oc continue control Resumes the last approved flow depends /oc stop control Halts current work, marks status:blocked no /oc explain <topic> read-only Explains an issue, a decision, or a design no /oc investigate <topic> read-only Investigates and reports findings no /oc status read-only Reports current state and recovery status no

docs.title: Targeting an agent
docs.text:
Prefix with @<agent> to direct the work to one logical agent. The orchestrator delegates to the named agent.

/oc @architect analyze the persistence options
/oc @qa verify the acceptance criteria
/oc @security review authorization
/oc @backend explain the Money rounding rule

Valid agent names:

orchestrator, brainstormer, product-planner, architect, backend-implementer, frontend-implementer, qa-engineer, code-reviewer, security-reviewer, documentation, researcher.

docs.title: Read-only vs. modifying commands
docs.text:
• Read-only (explain, investigate, status): run for any non-bot actor, with minimal permissions. Good for public discussions.
  • Modifying (analyze, brainstorm, plan, decide, implement, review, qa, continue, stop): only run for trusted actors* listed in the repository variable OC_TRUSTED_ACTORS. An untrusted request is rejected with a comment.

> analyze, review, qa can write reports/decisions or test artifacts, so they are treated as modifying for permission purposes.

Trigger phrases are case-insensitive (/OC, Oc are fine).

docs.title: Natural language is preserved
docs.text:
Everything after the command is kept. The agents read the full issue thread (description + all comments), so you do not need to restate the requirement.

/oc implement but use the simpler approach discussed by QA

The orchestrator receives the Issue, relevant comments, brainstorm report, decision, and your command. Your latest explicit instruction wins.

docs.title: Typical lifecycles
docs.text:
Feature:

1. Create the Issue (product description, acceptance criteria if you have them).
2. (optional) /oc analyze this issue
3. Wait for triage; the team brainstorms + posts a plan, marks status:ready.
4. /oc implement
5. OpenCode opens a PR; review it in the Files tab.
6. /oc qa, then /oc review (or reply to the auto-review)
7. Fix requests: "please address reviewer finding 2 in the PR", or /oc continue
8. Merge in the GitHub UI.

Reopen/recover:

/oc status            → what is happening? what should happen next?
/oc continue          → resume after a partial failure
/oc stop              → I want this paused right now

Decision override:

Human: /oc use option A instead

docs.title: What you see
docs.text:
• Status comments (🤖 STARTED, 🤖 COMPLETED, phase markers) on the Issue.
  • Concise agent comments with identity (Agent:, Run:).
  • Links to durable reports (docs/ai/brainstorms/, ADRs) instead of huge transcripts.
  • Commits carrying Agent: / Agent-Run: / Issue: trailers.
  • PRs with a Summary, Closes #N, AI Execution table, and Review status.
  • CI checks running mvn verify.

docs.title: Autopilot mode
docs.text:
When the repository variable AUTOPILOT == 'on', issues opened by trusted actors (in OC_TRUSTED_ACTORS) run the full chain without per-phase /oc commands — the opencode-pipeline.yml workflow self-dispatches each phase:

issue opened -> analyze (+brainstorm+plan) -> implement -> qa -> review+security
                     -> ready for human merge (you merge)
  • Each phase posts a status comment and advances the status:* labels.
  • status:blocked (or /oc stop) halts the chain; a human comment always overrides.
  • You still merge the PR — the agent team never merges by itself.
  • Manual activation: gh variable set AUTOPILOT --body on -R share-org/share (or the repo Settings → Secrets and variables → Variables UI).
  • Manual one-phase dispatch (e.g. after a fix): gh workflow run opencode-pipeline.yml -f issue=<N> -f phase=<phase> -R share-org/share.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• Do not paste instructions meant to bypass the trust model; commands are validated against OC_TRUSTED_ACTORS, not comment text.
  • Comments are not terminal transcripts: keep the thread concise; agents link to reports instead of dumping logs.
  • If a command seems to have done nothing, check the Actions tab for the workflow run, or run /oc status.

docs.title: MCP strategy
docs.text:
No MCP servers are configured during bootstrap. Nothing here invents server names, credentials, or URLs. This document defines intent and permissions for when MCP servers are added.

Only add MCP servers when they materially reduce repetitive context or provide controlled capabilities. Keep MCP documentation separate from agent logic.

docs.text:
Potential capabilities:

issues
pull requests
branches
repository metadata
checks/actions
comments

docs.title: Database MCP

docs.text:
• secrets stay outside repository files
  • least privilege

docs.title: Model strategy
docs.text: This repository uses explicit per-agent model assignments so that every role runs on a model suited to its workload. Roles are preserved even if a specific model identity is unavailable; unresolved models are documented here rather than silently replaced.

docs.title: Why the OpenRouter :free agents were remapped (2026-09-21, chore OPS-003)
docs.text:
During OPS-010 verification, subagent runs failed with a free-models-per-day rate-limit message ("add 10 credits to unlock 1000 free model requests per day"). The four agents that had been assigned OpenRouter :free models (backend-implementer, frontend-implementer, qa-engineer, code-reviewer) were remapped to the OpenCode gateway free tier (opencode/*-free, verified working anonymously — see OPS-002) to keep the roster consistent and avoid depending on mixed providers.

Honest caveat: this remap does NOT bypass the daily free-model cap. The free-models-per-day limit is enforced by the model gateway for free-tier requests across providers and was already exhausted during heavy sessions. If the daily cap blocks subagents again, options are: wait for the reset, add gateway credits (1000 free requests/day per the message), or use a paid OpenRouter low-cost model. The original OpenRouter assignments are recorded in the matrix above as the revert target if an OpenRouter subscription is added.

docs.title: Model resolution in GitHub Actions
docs.text:
GitHub workflows run the orchestrator as the primary agent and resolve the model passed to anomalyco/opencode/github@latest from .github/oc-models.json — the single source that mirrors the roster above. The workflows never override a per-agent model otherwise; targeted @agent work runs through the orchestrator's task tool with each subagent's own assigned model.

Runtime details:

  • Workflows use use_github_token: true (GITHUB_TOKEN mode), so no OpenCode GitHub App install is required and workflow permissions stay per-job (least privilege).
  • Model endpoints in the runner are intended to be the same opencode/*-free gateway verified in OPS-002. If the runner cannot reach the anonymous free tier, add the OPENCODE_API_KEY repository secret (OpenCode gateway/team key) or a provider secret such as ANTHROPIC_API_KEY, and update .github/oc-models.json plus this strategy together.
  • The free-tier daily cap documented below applies in CI as well; heavy GitHub-triggered runs may need gateway credits or a paid low-cost fallback.

docs.title: Cost profile
docs.text:
• Primary models are all free-tier or free-gateway models. The system is built for cheap/free operation.
  • :free OpenRouter models may carry rate-limit and concurrency constraints; expect them to be less reliable during peak usage.
  • Fallbacks 1 and 2 below are low-cost; fallback 3 is a paid model and is used only when configured.

docs.title: Fallback policy
docs.text:
Fallbacks are optional and depend on the model provider the developer has configured. Never hard-code a paid provider credential or API key.

When the primary model fails (unavailable endpoint, rate limit, repeated tool failure, context limitations, repeated unsuccessful implementation attempts):

  1. deepseek low-cost model available through the configured provider (e.g. openrouter/~deepseek/deepseek-flash-latest).
  2. glm low-cost model available through the configured provider (e.g. openrouter/~z-ai/glm-flash-latest).
  3. gpt-5.6-luna / the OpenAI luna family (e.g. openrouter/~openai/gpt-luna-latest) only as a final low-cost/high-capability fallback when configured.

Note: the literal identifier gpt-5.6-luna may not resolve in every installation; the ~openai/gpt-luna-latest alias is the supported spelling on OpenRouter. Verify availability with opencode models before use.

After two materially similar failures, escalate or change strategy rather than blindly retrying the same approach.

docs.title: Rate-limit considerations
docs.text:
• Free-tier endpoints commonly enforce per-minute/per-day limits. For planning agents (orchestrator, product-planner, architect) prefer fewer, larger calls over many small ones.
  • Keep agent prompts compact (see docs/ai/context-management.md) to stay within context limits and reduce token burn.

docs.title: Privacy considerations
docs.text:
Free does not automatically mean private.

  • Free third-party model endpoints may have provider-specific logging, training, and data-use policies.
  • Do not send secrets, tokens, credentials, or more data than necessary to any model endpoint.
  • Treat household financial data sent to any external model as sensitive. Where possible, prefer providers the team has verified, and keep prompts free of PII and credentials.
  • This document contains no secrets, tokens, or credentials.

docs.title: Unresolved items / human configuration
docs.text:
• Verified (2026-09-21, chore OPS-002): the opencode/*-free identifiers (opencode/nemotron-3-ultra-free, opencode/nemotron-3.5-lightning-free, opencode/ling-3.0-flash-fin-free) are served by the OpenCode gateway and respond anonymously — no API key or billing required for the free-tier models. They were probed with a one-turn opencode run --model ... check.
  • Verify all identifiers resolve locally: opencode models
  • After any change to agent/model configuration, restart OpenCode so the new configuration is loaded.

docs.title: Project Manager
docs.text:
The Autonomous Product & Engineering Manager owns the state and progress of the entire product. It sits above the orchestrator, which coordinates a single bounded execution.

The founder sets direction. The Project Manager controls execution.

docs.title: Role and authority
docs.text:
The manager answers, continuously:

Where are we?          Where should we be?     What is blocking us?
What should happen next?                       Who should do it?
Is the current work progressing?               Is the work actually complete?
What should be created next?

It owns the delivery loop. It does not own the product vision, and it does not implement code.

It may It may not Create and sequence issues Redefine the vision, MVP scope or business model Delegate specialists and the pipeline Implement or edit application source Maintain roadmap execution status Silently reverse an accepted ADR Evaluate gates and merge (subject to policy) Merge guardrail or CRITICAL changes Classify risk, set budgets, escalate Reach production in any way Close obsolete work, unblock stalled work Weaken tests, gates or security controls

docs.title: Hierarchy
docs.text:
HUMAN / FOUNDER
      |
      v
PROJECT MANAGER            <-- this agent
      |
 product-planner / architect / designer
      |
 backend-implementer / frontend-implementer
      |
 qa-engineer / code-reviewer / security-reviewer
      |
      v
  PR --> MANAGER GATE --> MERGE --> ROADMAP RECONCILE --> NEXT VALUE

The manager is a mode: primary agent invoked by its own heartbeat workflow. This is not a stylistic choice. The agent: input of anomalyco/opencode/github documents "Must be a primary agent" and falls back to build without any warning when the named agent is not one. While the manager was declared mode: subagent, the heartbeat passed agent: project-manager, silently ran as build, and the run log said agent: "build" from start to finish. Every permission in the manager's frontmatter was therefore inert: bash * was allowed (the file says * is deny), and external_directory fell back to the default ask instead of deny. The ask action has nobody to answer it in CI, so the cycle blocked until its step timeout — 80 minutes to do nothing.

Two rules follow, and both are enforced by scripts/test-project-manager.sh:

  • An agent named in a workflow's agent: input must be mode: primary. Otherwise that workflow runs as build with its permissions.
  • ask is deny in CI. An unattended cycle must never wait on a decision.

The manager is conceptually above the orchestrator and both are primary entry points. Only two agents in the roster are primary: the orchestrator and the manager.

docs.title: The reconciliation cycle
docs.text:
Run on every heartbeat and every event trigger. Full derivation rules are in docs/ai/project-state.md.

  1. Reconstruct state — ledger, issues by label, open PRs, CI, recent merges, blocked work, prototype feedback, roadmap. Staged and filtered; never a full repository read.
  2. Compare reality to the roadmap — classify each capability as completed, in-progress, blocked, missing, obsolete or next.
  3. Detect bottlenecks — work waiting on UX, PRs waiting on QA, repeated QA failure, missing spec or ADR, stranded agents, blocking dependencies, budget exhaustion, unprocessed feedback.
  4. Act — the smallest useful action, preferring to unblock existing work over creating new work.
  5. Verify and record — write state back to the ledger; comment on GitHub only when something meaningful changed.

docs.title: Proactive, but never busy
docs.text:
Idle detection is required. If nothing is active and the roadmap has unblocked value, the manager starts it without waiting to be asked.

Creating work to look busy is forbidden. If the correct action is to do nothing, the manager does nothing and says so. This is enforced three ways: the per-cycle issue cap, the requirement that a new issue pass a seven-point pre-flight check, and the explicit prompt rule.

Before creating any issue the manager must: search open issues, search closed issues, check the roadmap, check in-flight work, confirm the work is genuinely needed, confirm it is not already covered, and confirm it is actionable now.

docs.title: Completion requires evidence
docs.text:
requirements satisfied AND implementation complete AND tests pass
AND QA passed AND review passed AND CI green
AND required UX validation passed AND required documentation updated

An agent saying "done" is a claim, not evidence. Levels of completion — task, feature, milestone, MVP, product — are tracked separately; see docs/product/done-criteria.md.

docs.title: Delegation
docs.text:
Delegation is GitHub-native: the manager decides what should run and hands it to opencode-pipeline.yml, which executes each specialist as its own job. Specialists never run inside the manager's cycle — task is deny in both the manager and the orchestrator for exactly this reason. When the manager ran with task available it spawned subagents inside its own job (run 36325854323 shows agent: "backend-implementer" at 14:31:20, nested inside the orchestrator's run). A nested agent shares its parent's timeout, so one hung subagent consumes the entire cycle, and the pipeline's own concurrency group, state machine and merge gates are bypassed.

Two mechanisms, both labelling at creation time:

# New work: labels MUST be in the same call as the create.
gh issue create --title "..." --body "..." \
  --label "status:ready" --label "agent:created"

# Existing issue:
gh workflow run opencode-pipeline.yml --repo "$GITHUB_REPOSITORY" \
  -f issue=<N> -f phase=analyze

Label atomicity is not a style rule. The pipeline guard reads labels at event time (github.event.issue.labels). Create-then-label fires the event with no labels, so the issue seeds at analyze instead of implement — silently, one phase off, for every issue the manager ever creates.

Pass only the issue number and the phase. Each phase re-reads live GitHub state, so context pasted into the prompt is stale on arrival.

Smallest sufficient team, by work type:

Work Chain UX / prototype feedback designer → frontend-implementer → qa-engineer New feature product-planner → architect → implementer → qa-engineer → code-reviewer Security-sensitive architect → security-reviewer → implementer → qa-engineer → code-reviewer Money / financial logic product-planner → architect → backend-implementer → qa-engineer → security-reviewer Documentation only documentation External research only researcher

docs.title: PR handling
docs.text:
The manager monitors every open PR for CI failure, review findings, QA failure, merge conflicts, staleness, and missing description, tests or issue link. It reads the failure, classifies it, delegates the correction, and lets CI re-run. It never resolves a red build by merging it.

Review findings follow the same loop: classify → delegate correction → QA → re-review. The founder should not have to tell an agent to fix each comment.

docs.title: Merge policy
docs.text:
Merging is the highest-risk action the manager takes, and the full gate list plus the absolute prohibitions live in .opencode/agents/project-manager.md and docs/ai/autonomy-policy.md.

The manager merges implementation PRs directly once every gate passes. This was an explicit owner decision against the recommended design of delegating to the pipeline's auto-merge step; the reasoning, the accepted costs, and the fallback path are recorded in docs/architecture/decisions/ADR-002-autonomous-project-manager.md.

Permanent carve-outs at every autonomy level:

  • guardrail changes (.github/, .opencode/, AGENTS.md, oc-models.json) are merged by the founder, by hand
  • risk:critical is propose-only
  • never --admin, never bypass branch protection, never force-push main
  • never weaken a test, a gate or a security control to make work pass

Reducing MANAGER_AUTONOMY to supervised makes the manager stop before merge with no code change.

docs.title: Autonomy, risk and budget
docs.text:
• docs/ai/autonomy-policy.md — modes, risk classes, financial-domain rules
  • docs/ai/autonomy-budget.md — numeric limits and failure/retry budgets

docs.title: Emergency stop
docs.text:
label manager:paused   on any open issue   -> scheduled runs exit without new work
MANAGER_AUTONOMY=human_only                 -> analysis and proposals only

A stop signal that still starts work is not a stop signal; PAUSED and EMERGENCY_STOP must produce zero new issues, zero delegations and zero merges.

Human commands, defined in .opencode/commands/manager.md and routed by .github/workflows/opencode-command.yml: /oc manager status, /oc manager pause, /oc manager resume, /oc manager run.

status is read-only and runs for any non-bot actor. The other three change state, so they run only for actors in OC_TRUSTED_ACTORS. pause and resume move the manager:paused label on the current issue. run asks the agent for one cycle; it does not bypass the shell gate, which is why a paused manager stays paused through it.

docs.title: Durable state
docs.text: There is no private backlog. Project state is derived from GitHub, and the manager's own bookkeeping (run log, budget counters, retry attempts, queued work) lives in a single pinned Manager Ledger issue. A manager that restarts from zero reconstructs everything it needs from GitHub and the repository.

docs.title: Reporting
docs.text: Routine cycle output goes to the ledger every run. GitHub comments are posted only for meaningful state changes. Durable reports, when a change warrants one, land in docs/ai/reports/ — see the README there for the convention and the "avoid excessive commits" rule.

docs.title: Model strategy
docs.text: The manager runs a reasoning model and delegates execution to the coding models, preserving the existing multi-model architecture. See docs/ai/model-strategy.md.

docs.title: Project State Model
docs.text:
How the Project Manager derives project state.

This is not a status file. Nothing here is edited by hand to record progress, and there is no machine-written state file in the repository. State is derived, on every run, from GitHub and the repository artifacts. This document describes the derivation so any human or agent can reproduce it.

The reason this matters: the manager is a transient process. It must be able to start from zero and reconstruct the project. If state lived only in a model's context, a restart would silently lose it — and a manager that cannot remember what it already did will duplicate work.

docs.title: Sources of truth, in precedence order
docs.text:
1. Human instruction — a direct comment from the founder. Always wins.
  2. GitHub labels on issues — authoritative for the state of actual work.
  3. Merged PRs and green CI — authoritative for what is genuinely complete.
  4. docs/product/done-criteria.md — authoritative for "product done".
  5. docs/product/roadmap.md — authoritative for intended order and scope. Its execution-status column is a mirror maintained by the manager.
  6. docs/architecture/decisions/ — authoritative for settled decisions.
  7. docs/product/mvp.md, vision.md, docs/ux/, docs/ai/ — context.

When two sources disagree, the higher one wins and the lower one is corrected. Labels beating the roadmap is the common case: the roadmap is documentation, the labels are reality.

docs.title: Work state machine
docs.text:
BACKLOG
   ↓
DISCOVERY      (analysis, and brainstorming when a design decision matters)
   ↓
DESIGN         (product-planner + architect; UX via designer when relevant)
   ↓
READY          (specified and actionable — safe for an implementer to start)
   ↓
IN_PROGRESS    (an implementation agent is working, or a PR is open)
   ↓
QA             (qa-engineer verifying acceptance criteria)
   ↓
REVIEW         (code review, plus security review when required)
   ↓
READY_TO_MERGE (all gates green; merge-eligible, or awaiting the founder)
   ↓
DONE

BLOCKED is a side state, not a step:

any state → BLOCKED → (resume) the state it came from

BLOCKED always carries evidence: what was tried, what failed, and what is needed. It is a legitimate outcome, not a failure to be avoided.

docs.title: Label mapping
docs.text:
State Label BACKLOG status:backlog DISCOVERY status:discovery DESIGN status:discovery (the design and analysis labels are intentionally the same) READY status:ready IN_PROGRESS status:in-progress QA status:qa REVIEW status:review READY_TO_MERGE status:qa + status:review DONE status:done BLOCKED status:blocked

Labels are created by scripts/setup-labels.sh.

docs.title: Manager state
docs.text:
The manager's own bookkeeping — run log, budget counters, retry attempts, queued work — lives in a single Manager Ledger issue. An issue was chosen over a repository file because it is atomic, auditable, visible to the founder, and already covered by the label and concurrency machinery.

"Pinned" here means identified by the manager:ledger label and never duplicated, not a GitHub UI pin: GitHub exposes no REST API for pinning issues, so the label is the only stable handle automation can resolve. The workflow finds the ledger by that label and creates it if it is missing, which makes "exactly one ledger" an invariant worth asserting rather than assuming.

The ledger is the answer to "what did the manager already do, so it does not do it twice". Before any create/dispatch/merge, the manager checks it.

docs.title: Deriving the current state
docs.text:
On each cycle the manager reads, in this order and no further:

  1. docs/ai/project-state.md (this file) and docs/ai/autonomy-policy.md
  2. the ledger issue
  3. issues filtered by state label — open ones, and status:blocked ones
  4. open PRs and their CI status
  5. recent merges (last ~20)
  6. prototype feedback issues
  7. docs/product/roadmap.md
  8. only then the specific files for the work in hand

Filter by label before sending anything to a model. Reading every issue is both slow and a context-economics violation; the whole point of labels is that they let the manager select rather than ingest.

docs.title: Deriving progress against the roadmap
docs.text:
For each roadmap capability, classify using evidence rather than assertion:

Classification Evidence required completed a merged PR and green CI and the acceptance criteria demonstrably met in-progress an open issue in READY..REVIEW, or an open PR blocked status:blocked with recorded evidence missing no issue covers it obsolete superseded by a decision, or explicitly out of MVP scope next the earliest missing or obsolete-but-still-wanted capability whose dependencies are all completed

next is the answer to "what should happen next", and it is the only input to the proactive-work decision. Dependencies come from the roadmap ordering and from Part of / feedback:child-of- relationships on issues.

docs.title: Deriving quality state
docs.text:
CI failing on any open PR   → the owning issue is not progressing
QA failed or never ran      → the PR is not merge-eligible
review finding open         → delegate the correction, do not merge
security review absent on a HIGH/CRITICAL change → not merge-eligible

docs.title: Deriving "is it actually complete"
docs.text:
A task is DONE only with all of:

requirements satisfied
AND implementation complete
AND tests pass
AND QA passed
AND review passed
AND CI green
AND required UX / visual validation passed
AND required documentation updated

An agent reporting "done" is a claim, not evidence. The manager verifies against merged PRs, CI and QA results.

Completion is also a ladder, and the levels must not be conflated:

task done      → this issue's acceptance criteria are met
feature done   → the user-visible capability works end to end
milestone done → every capability in the milestone is done
MVP done       → every MVP capability in docs/product/mvp.md is done
product done   → docs/product/done-criteria.md is satisfied

Only the last one means the project is finished.

docs.title: Anti-patterns this model exists to prevent
docs.text:
• Treating a merged PR as a completed feature.
  • Treating "no open issues" as "nothing left to do" when the roadmap has more.
  • Creating a duplicate task because the previous one was described in different words — hence: search open and closed issues before creating.
  • Keeping a private backlog in model context that no human can audit.

docs.title: Brainstorming reports
docs.text:
This directory stores durable brainstorming decision reports.

Naming convention:

BR-001-<short-topic>.md
BR-002-<short-topic>.md
...

Use the next number after the highest existing report.

Every report:

  • references its GitHub Issue (Issue: #123)
  • follows the template in .opencode/skills/brainstorming/SKILL.md
  • is a decision artifact (concise), not a transcript of the agent discussion
  • records the selected solution, alternatives, trade-offs, risks, and confidence

Brainstorm reports are problem analysis. Long-term architectural decisions are recorded separately as ADRs in docs/architecture/decisions/.

No brainstorming reports exist yet; the first design discussion will create BR-001-<topic>.md.

docs.title: Metadata
docs.text: Issue: #5 (https://github.com/share-org/share/issues/5) Date: 2026-09-21 Participants: security-reviewer, backend-implementer, qa-engineer, code-reviewer Status: DECIDED

docs.title: Problem
docs.text:
The OpenCode agent permission architecture has two critical inconsistencies identified in the baseline code review (issue #2):

  • C1: .opencode/agents/qa-engineer.md has unrestricted bash: allow — the most dangerous permission in the roster, inconsistent with every other agent (orchestrator, code-reviewer, security-reviewer use git *: allow, *: deny).
  • C2: .opencode/agents/backend-implementer.md and .opencode/agents/frontend-implementer.md have NO permission: block at all — the two write-capable implementation agents are the least constrained and least documented.

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
• 11 agents total: 1 primary (orchestrator) + 10 subagents
  • 8 agents already have proper restrictive permissions following a consistent pattern
  • 3 agents are problematic (qa-engineer, backend-implementer, frontend-implementer)
  • Repository is a modular monolith with mandatory household isolation (AGENTS.md)
  • Agents never merge production code automatically
  • AGENTS.md security rules: "Never give database write access to unknown/untrusted clients", "Household isolation is mandatory"

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• Must follow least-privilege principle
  • Must be consistent across the roster (follow orchestrator/code-reviewer/security-reviewer pattern)
  • Must not break agent functionality (implementers need to write code, QA needs to run tests)
  • Fix must be minimal and follow existing patterns
  • Valid permission keys per config schema: read, edit, write, glob, grep, list, bash, task, external_directory, todowrite, question, webfetch, websearch, lsp, doom_loop, skill

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: Agent Functional Needs backend-implementer Read/edit/write Java/Spring files, Maven config, run mvn commands, read database migrations frontend-implementer Read/edit/write React/TypeScript files in frontend/, run npm/npx commands qa-engineer Run tests (Maven, npm), read test results, inspect code — NO write access needed

docs.title: Unknowns / Assumptions
docs.text:
• Assumption: Implementers don't need arbitrary shell; only standard build/test commands (mvn *, npm *, npx *)
  • Assumption: task tool not needed (implementers don't delegate in current workflow)
  • Assumption: webfetch/websearch not needed for any of these three agents
  • Unknown: Whether backend may occasionally need to edit files outside src/** (e.g., Docker, scripts) — mitigated by explicit pom.xml allow and extensible pattern

docs.title: Option A: Security-Reviewer (Strict Path Scoping)
docs.text:
Description: Narrow path allowlists (src/main/java/**, src/test/java/** for backend; frontend/** for frontend); bash restricted to mvn */npm *; QA gets test-only bash (mvn test*, npm test*).

Advantages: Strongest security posture; minimal attack surface; consistent with review agents.

Disadvantages: Backend path too narrow (misses src/main/resources, config, new modules); QA bash too restrictive (blocks mvn clean, mvn dependency:tree).

Risks: Legitimate development workflows blocked; frequent permission updates needed.

docs.title: Option B: Backend-Implementer (Broad Permissive)
docs.text:
Description: edit: allow, write: allow for backend; file-type patterns for frontend; bash allowlist for build commands.

Advantages: Zero friction for legitimate work; simple.

Disadvantages: Violates least privilege — edit: allow/write: allow with no path restrictions allows modification of agent configs, security docs, frontend code, any file. Inconsistent with roster.

Risks: HIGH — contradicts AGENTS.md principle applied to agents; security regression.

docs.title: Option C: QA-Engineer (File-Type Patterns + Test-Focused)
docs.text:
Description: File-type patterns (**/*.java, **/pom.xml, **/*.yml) for backend; QA has zero write; test-scoped bash allowlist.

Advantages: QA write-zero is correct; file-type patterns handle new files; test-focused bash.

Disadvantages: **/*.yml too broad (allows CI/CD, docker-compose); file-type patterns miss non-standard extensions; no sensitive path denies.

Risks: Medium — accidental modification of infrastructure config.

docs.title: Option D: Code-Reviewer (Pattern Consistency + Defense-in-Depth) ← SELECTED BASE
docs.text:
Description: Exact orchestrator pattern (map + *: deny fallback) for all tools; src/** + pom.xml for backend with explicit denies for .opencode/**, docs/architecture/security.md; frontend/** for frontend with same sensitive denies; QA gets mvn */npm * bash; explicit denies for webfetch, websearch, task, skill, external_directory.

Advantages: Maximum consistency; defense-in-depth; explicit audit trail; follows established convention.

Disadvantages: Most verbose; sensitive path deny list maintenance.

Risks: Low — denies are additive safety; can extend allowlist if needed.

docs.title: Discussion
docs.text:
Key disagreements recorded:

  1. Backend file scope: Security-Reviewer (narrow src/main/java/**) vs Backend-Implementer (broad edit: allow) vs Code-Reviewer (src/** with sensitive denies) vs QA-Engineer (file-type **/*.java). Resolution: src/** with sensitive denies balances practicality and safety.

  2. QA bash scope: Security-Reviewer/Code-Reviewer (mvn *, npm *) vs QA-Engineer (test-only mvn test*). Resolution: Broader mvn */npm * — QA needs clean, dependency:tree, etc.

  3. Tool exclusions: Only Code-Reviewer proposed explicit webfetch/websearch/task/skill denies. Resolution: Include explicit denies for clarity and audit.

  4. Sensitive path denies: Only Code-Reviewer proposed .opencode/** and docs/architecture/security.md denies. Resolution: Include for defense-in-depth.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: Selected solution: Refined Option D (Code-Reviewer base with adjustments from critique).

  write:

docs.text:
permission:
  read: allow
  glob: allow
  grep: allow
  list: allow
  edit:
    "frontend/**": allow
    ".opencode/**": deny
    "docs/architecture/security.md": deny

  write:
    "frontend/**": allow

  webfetch: deny
  websearch: deny
  task: deny
  skill: deny

docs.title: Why
docs.text:
• Consistency: Matches the orchestrator/code-reviewer/security-reviewer pattern exactly (map form with allowlist + *: deny fallback).
  • Least privilege: Each agent gets only what it needs; no unrestricted bash, no broad edit: allow.
  • Defense-in-depth: Explicit denies for sensitive paths (agent configs, security docs) prevent accidental/malicious modification.
  • Explicit tool denies: Clarifies that webfetch/websearch/task/skill/external_directory are not needed.
  • Practical: src/** and frontend/** cover legitimate work including new modules/files; mvn */npm * cover all build/test scenarios.

docs.title: Trade-offs
docs.text: Trade-off Decision Verbosity vs. clarity Accept verbosity for clarity and auditability src/** breadth vs. narrow src/main/java/** src/** preferred (covers resources, test fixtures, new modules); sensitive denies mitigate risk Explicit tool denies vs. implicit Explicit denies for documentation and audit trail Sensitive path deny list maintenance Accept maintenance burden for defense-in-depth

docs.title: Risks
docs.text:
1. Backend may need files outside src/** (Docker, scripts, root config). Mitigation: pom.xml explicitly allowed; rare cases can extend allowlist.
  2. Build command evolution (wrapper scripts, new npm commands). Mitigation: mvn * covers wrapper; npm * covers all npm.
  3. QA may need non-Maven/npm commands (docker, psql). Mitigation: Not in current scope; extend if needed.

docs.title: Rejected Alternatives
docs.text: Alternative Reason Backend-Implementer's edit: allow, write: allow Violates least privilege; inconsistent; security risk Security-Reviewer's narrow src/main/java/** Too restrictive; breaks legitimate work (resources, test fixtures) QA-Engineer's test-only bash (mvn test*) Too restrictive; QA needs mvn clean, mvn dependency:tree Omitting explicit webfetch/websearch/task denies Implicit deny per schema, but explicit is clearer for audit File-type patterns (**/*.java) Misses non-standard extensions; directory patterns more maintainable

docs.title: Follow-up
docs.text:
• Apply the three permission blocks to their respective agent files
  • Verify agents can still perform their duties (run a test task for each)
  • Consider whether architect and product-planner should get bash: { "git *": allow, "*": deny } for consistency (currently they have no bash at all)

docs.title: Confidence
docs.text: HIGH — The solution follows the established pattern in the repository, applies least privilege consistently, addresses both C1 and C2 findings, and the trade-offs are well-understood. The only uncertainty is whether any edge-case file paths are missed, but the pattern allows easy extension.

docs.text: Issue: #3 (feat EXP-105 : expense shares) Date: 2026-09-22 Participants: backend-implementer, architect, security-reviewer, domain-modeler Status: COMPLETED

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Implement expense sharing across household members with explicit separation of: who paid, who participated, who owes, allocation method, and how a debt was settled.

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
• MVP supports EQUAL and CUSTOM splits (roadmap includes PERCENTAGE and SHARES for Phase 2)
  • Domain model defines: Household, Member, Expense, Money, Allocation, Balance, Settlement
  • Money value object exists with BigDecimal, explicit currency, HALF_UP rounding to 2 decimal places
  • Household isolation is mandatory (security.md)
  • PostgreSQL is the transactional source of truth
  • Modular monolith architecture with domain/application/infrastructure separation

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• Never use double/float for monetary values
  • Currency must be explicit
  • Rounding rules must be defined and tested
  • Household isolation: member must not access another household's data by changing identifier
  • Domain must not depend on Spring or database implementation details
  • Keep business logic out of controllers

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
1. Expense belongs to exactly one household
  2. Payer must be a household member
  3. Participants must be household members
  4. Allocations cannot be negative
  5. Total allocation must equal expense total (with deterministic rounding policy)
  6. Split methods: EQUAL, PERCENTAGE, SHARES, CUSTOM
  7. Audit/history strategy for expense editing

docs.title: Unknowns / Assumptions
docs.text:
• Exact rounding policy for allocation remainder distribution
  • Whether allocations are stored as derived values or computed on read
  • API contract shape for creating expenses with different split methods
  • Database schema for expense, allocation, participant relationships
  • How to handle expense editing while preserving audit trail
  • Whether to implement all split methods now or phase them

docs.title: Option A: Backend Implementer (Implementation-First)
docs.text:
Description: Explicit persisted allocations for all split methods. Strategy pattern in ExpenseAllocationService with HALF_UP rounding, remainder to first N by memberId. Single API endpoint. Database: expense + expense_allocation tables.

Advantages: Clear separation, testable, extensible, supports audit, simple remainder handling

Disadvantages: More database rows, allocation service needs careful edge-case testing

Risks: Rounding edge cases with many participants; service becoming god object

docs.title: Option B: Architect (Architecture-First)
docs.text:
Description: Hybrid computed (EQUAL/PERCENTAGE) vs persisted (CUSTOM/SHARES) allocations. Largest remainder (Hamilton) rounding. Separate authorization service. Clean layer separation.

Advantages: Clean architecture, fair rounding, optimized storage, explicit authorization boundary

Disadvantages: Hybrid complexity, two code paths, largest remainder harder to implement

Risks: Inconsistency between computed/persisted; authorization gaps

docs.title: Option C: Security Reviewer (Isolation-First)
docs.text:
Description: Application-layer authorization + PostgreSQL RLS as defense-in-depth. Pure domain allocation functions. Event sourcing for audit trail from day one.

Advantages: Strong isolation, audit built-in, pure domain logic, RLS safety net

Disadvantages: RLS couples to PostgreSQL, event sourcing overkill for MVP, more infrastructure

Risks: RLS performance; event table growth; authorization bottleneck

docs.title: Option D: Domain Modeler (Domain-First)
docs.text:
Description: Invariants in Expense aggregate. SplitMethod enum with factories. Banker's rounding (HALF_EVEN). Payer receives remainder. Separate BalanceCalculator.

Advantages: Strong invariants, encapsulated logic, intuitive payer-remainder, clean separation

Disadvantages: Payer-remainder may seem unfair; HALF_EVEN inconsistent with Money; enum bloat

Risks: Enum bloat; remainder policy disputes; invariant validation performance

docs.title: Discussion
docs.text:
Key disagreements and resolutions:

  1. Persisted vs computed allocations: All specialists except Architect favored uniform persisted allocations. Architect's hybrid approach was rejected due to double code paths, audit complexity, and inconsistency risk. Storage cost is negligible for household scale.

  2. Rounding method: Money class uses HALF_UP. Domain Modeler proposed HALF_EVEN (banker's rounding) but this creates inconsistency. Architect proposed largest remainder (mathematically fair but complex). Consensus: HALF_UP consistently, remainder to first N by deterministic memberId ordering.

  3. Payer-remainder vs first-N remainder: Domain Modeler argued payer should get remainder (intuitive). Others argued this is arbitrary and may confuse users. First-N by memberId is more explainable and testable.

  4. RLS and event sourcing: Security Reviewer advocated for both as defense-in-depth. Others rejected as over-engineering for MVP, coupling domain to PostgreSQL, and YAGNI. Application-layer authorization with AOP is sufficient.

  5. SplitMethod enum factories: Domain Modeler proposed factories on enum. Backend Implementer and Architect argued this bloats the enum; allocation logic belongs in domain service/factory.

  6. Authorization enforcement: Consensus on application-layer checks via HouseholdAuthorizationService + Spring AOP interceptor. Repository methods require householdId parameter. RLS deferred.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: Selected solution: Uniform persisted allocations with HALF_UP rounding, remainder to first N by memberId, Expense factory encapsulating allocation creation, application-layer authorization with AOP, single API endpoint, deferred RLS/event sourcing.

docs.title: Why
docs.text:
1. Persisted allocations uniformly - simplest, supports audit/editing, negligible storage cost
  2. HALF_UP rounding consistently - matches existing Money class, no dual rounding modes
  3. Deterministic remainder distribution - by memberId ordering is explainable and testable
  4. Expense factory encapsulates allocation creation - keeps invariants in aggregate, follows DDD
  5. Application-layer authorization with AOP - clean, testable, no PostgreSQL coupling
  6. Single API endpoint with discriminator - simpler routing, extensible
  7. Deferred event sourcing/RLS - YAGNI for MVP, can add later

docs.title: Trade-offs
docs.text: Decision Trade-off Persist all allocations Slightly more rows, but uniform code and audit support Remainder to first N by memberId Not "fairest" mathematically, but deterministic and explainable Single API endpoint Slightly more complex request validation, but simpler routing No RLS/event sourcing Relies on application correctness; mitigated by tests and AOP HALF_UP only Consistent with Money; no banker's rounding complexity

docs.title: Rejected Alternatives
docs.text:
1. Hybrid computed/persisted allocations - double code paths, audit complexity, inconsistency risk
  2. Largest remainder rounding - harder to explain, more complex implementation
  3. Payer receives remainder - arbitrary, may confuse users
  4. Banker's rounding (HALF_EVEN) - inconsistent with Money class
  5. RLS + Event Sourcing - over-engineering for MVP, couples domain to PostgreSQL
  6. SplitMethod enum factories - bloats enum, allocation logic belongs in domain service/factory

docs.title: Risks
docs.text:
1. Rounding edge cases - Mitigation: comprehensive unit tests for all split methods
  2. Authorization gaps - Mitigation: AOP interceptor + repository contract + integration tests
  3. Allocation service complexity - Mitigation: strategy pattern with separate class per split method
  4. Expense editing audit - Mitigation: updated_by/updated_at for MVP; design for future event table

docs.title: Open Questions
docs.text:
1. Should ExpenseAllocationService be in domain or application layer? (Currently domain)
  2. How to handle expense deletion? Soft delete (status) or hard delete? (Hard delete with FK cascade for MVP)
  3. Should participantIds be derivable from allocations? (Yes for EQUAL/PERCENTAGE/SHARES; explicit for CUSTOM)

docs.title: Confidence
docs.text: HIGH - Strong alignment across specialists on core decisions. Clear precedent from existing Money class and domain model documentation. Well-understood problem space with bounded scope (MVP: EQUAL + CUSTOM).
