docs.text: Issue: #9 (https://github.com/share-org/share/issues/9) Date: 2026-09-25 Participants: documentation, architect, security-reviewer, orchestrator Status: DECIDED

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: The docs/ai/mcp-strategy.md document contains a "Recommended permissions by agent" table (lines 45-99) that defines MCP server capabilities per agent. This table appears to conflict with actual agent frontmatter permissions in .opencode/agents/*.md. The issue asks to either label the MCP permissions as "aspirational" or align the frontmatter — but these are fundamentally different permission models operating at different layers.

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
• MCP permissions (mcp-strategy.md): Future-facing definitions of what MCP server capabilities agents should have when MCP servers are configured (GitHub, Database, Repository, CI, Production, Web access). The document header states: "No MCP servers are configured during bootstrap. Nothing here invents server names, credentials, or URLs. This document defines intent and permissions for when MCP servers are added."
  • Frontmatter permissions (agent files): Current OpenCode tool permissions controlling what tools agents can use during execution (read, edit, write, bash, webfetch, websearch, task, etc.). These were recently updated per ADR-001 (Issue #5) to follow a consistent least-privilege pattern.
  • BR-001 / ADR-001: Already resolved the OpenCode agent permission architecture. The three problematic agents (qa-engineer, backend-implementer, frontend-implementer) now have restrictive, consistent permission blocks.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• Must not conflate two different permission models
  • Must preserve the aspirational/forward-looking nature of MCP strategy
  • Must not retroactively change ADR-001 decisions
  • Must be clear to future readers/maintainers

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• mcp-strategy.md must accurately reflect its purpose (intent for future MCP servers)
  • Agent frontmatter must accurately reflect current OpenCode tool permissions
  • No false equivalence between the two models

docs.title: Unknowns / Assumptions
docs.text:
• Assumption: The MCP strategy will eventually be implemented; the table serves as a design target.
  • Unknown: Exact MCP server capabilities when implemented.
  • Unknown: Whether any future MCP server integration will map directly to current frontmatter tools.

docs.title: Option A: Documentation Agent — Table Note Only
docs.text:
Description: Add an explicit header note above the "Recommended permissions by agent" table stating these are aspirational MCP server capability definitions — not current OpenCode tool permissions.

Advantages: Minimal change; preserves all existing MCP permission definitions; eliminates false equivalence; honest about aspirational nature.

Disadvantages: Doesn't remove the table (which some might still find confusing); note might be missed.

Risks: Low — purely documentation clarification.

docs.title: Option B: Architect — Two-Layer Architecture Section
docs.text:
Description: Formally distinguish the two permission layers in the document structure: Layer 1 (OpenCode Tool Permissions, current) and Layer 2 (MCP Server Capabilities, future). Add a "Permission Model Layers" section explaining this distinction.

Advantages: Architecturally sound separation of concerns; future-proof; prevents category errors in future decisions.

Disadvantages: More verbose; may be over-engineering for current needs; adds documentation maintenance burden.

Risks: Medium — adds maintenance surface; premature for pre-implementation docs.

docs.title: Option C: Security Reviewer — Explicit "Not Enforced" Label
docs.text:
Description: Label the table explicitly as "Aspirational MCP Capabilities (Not Enforced)" and add a security note referencing ADR-001 as the current enforcement authority.

Advantages: Security-audit friendly; clear enforcement boundary; reinforces ADR-001 as current authority.

Disadvantages: "Not Enforced" could be misread as "these don't matter" rather than "future design."

Risks: Low — improves security clarity; slight risk of discouraging future MCP implementation.

docs.title: Option D: Orchestrator — Header Rename + Preamble (SELECTED)
docs.text:
Description: Replace the section header "## Recommended permissions by agent" with "## Aspirational MCP Server Capabilities by Agent (Future)" and add a one-sentence preamble cross-referencing ADR-001 and frontmatter.

Advantages: Highest leverage (header is most visible); fixes mental model at source; zero maintenance; works for human and agent consumers; audit-friendly.

Disadvantages: Doesn't add architectural depth (not needed for this fix).

Risks: Very low — purely a label change.

docs.title: Discussion
docs.text:
Key disagreements recorded:

  1. Structural vs. minimal fix: Architect preferred a two-layer architectural explanation; others preferred minimal label fix. Resolution: Minimal fix now; structural docs (ADR) later if MCP implementation proceeds.

  2. "Not Enforced" vs. "Aspirational" framing: Security reviewer favored "Not Enforced" for audit clarity; others preferred "Aspirational... (Future)" as constructive forward-looking framing. Resolution: "Aspirational... (Future)" + "design intent" language — more constructive, still audit-clear.

  3. Table content changes: No participant proposed changing the table content — all agreed it correctly represents future design intent.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: Selected solution: Option D (Orchestrator) — Header rename + preamble sentence.

docs.title: Concrete Changes to docs/ai/mcp-strategy.md
docs.text:
1. Line 45: Change ## Recommended permissions by agent → ## Aspirational MCP Server Capabilities by Agent (Future)

  2. After line 45 (new line 46): Add preamble:

    The following table defines intended MCP server capabilities for each agent when MCP servers are configured. These are NOT current OpenCode tool permissions (defined in agent frontmatter per ADR-001). The two permission models operate independently: frontmatter controls OpenCode tool access during execution; this table expresses design intent for future MCP server integration.

  3. Table content (lines 47-99): Unchanged.

docs.title: Why
docs.text:
• Root cause addressed: The ambiguous header "Recommended permissions by agent" is the primary confusion vector. Renaming it fixes the mental model at the highest visibility point.
  • Minimal and surgical: One header change + one sentence. No table edits, no structural reorganization.
  • Audit-friendly: Explicitly references ADR-001 as the current authority, draws clear enforcement boundary.
  • Future-proof: "Aspirational... (Future)" and "design intent" language remains accurate regardless of MCP implementation timeline.
  • Agent-readable: The orchestrator and other agents parsing this document will encounter the clarified header first.

docs.title: Trade-offs
docs.text: Trade-off Decision Minimal fix vs. architectural depth Minimal fix now; architectural doc (ADR) later if MCP implementation proceeds Explicit "Not Enforced" vs. "Aspirational/Design Intent" "Aspirational... (Future)" + "design intent" — constructive forward-looking framing Header-only vs. header + body notes Header + one-sentence preamble strikes the right balance

docs.title: Risks
docs.text:
1. Low: Future reader might still confuse the models despite clarification. Mitigation: The preamble explicitly cross-references ADR-001 and frontmatter.
  2. Low: MCP implementation diverges from this table. Mitigation: Table is explicitly labeled "aspirational" and "design intent" — divergence is expected.
  3. None: No runtime behavior changes; purely documentation.

docs.title: Rejected Alternatives
docs.text: Alternative Reason Add table note only (Option A) Header remains misleading; note easily missed Two-layer architecture section (Option B) Over-engineering for a label confusion; premature for pre-implementation docs "Not Enforced" label only (Option C) Could discourage future work; doesn't fix header ambiguity Align frontmatter to MCP table Category error — different models, different layers, different purposes Delete the table Loses valuable design intent for future MCP work

docs.title: Follow-up
docs.text:
• Apply the two changes to docs/ai/mcp-strategy.md
  • No ADR needed — this is a documentation clarification, not an architectural decision
  • If MCP server implementation begins in the future, consider an ADR formalizing the two-layer permission model

docs.title: Confidence
docs.text: HIGH — The problem is a documentation labeling ambiguity between two clearly distinct permission models. The fix is minimal, addresses the root cause (ambiguous header), preserves all design intent, references the authoritative current permission decision (ADR-001), and introduces no runtime risk.

docs.text: Issue: #36 Date: 2026-09-27 Participants: orchestrator, architect Status: COMPLETED

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: The anomalyco/opencode/github@latest action starts with an unauthenticated curl to https://api.github.com/repos/anomalyco/opencode/releases/latest to get the latest version. On GitHub-hosted runners (shared IPs), this hits the 60 req/hr unauthenticated rate limit and fails with exit code 22, causing the entire action to abort before installing opencode. All 7 workflows in this repo use this action, so no agent job has ever run successfully.

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
• 7 workflows use uses: anomalyco/opencode/github@latest:
  • project-manager-loop.yml (line 189)
  • opencode-pr-review.yml (line 57)
  • opencode-command.yml (lines 160, 214, 286)
  • opencode-pipeline.yml (line 168)
  • opencode-prototype-feedback.yml (line 175)
  • opencode-issue-triage.yml (line 70)
  • opencode-agent-status.yml (line 47)
  • The action exposes NO input to pin or skip the version lookup
  • We cannot modify the upstream action (third-party)
  • The action runs with GITHUB_TOKEN available in env
  • Current fallback version=${VERSION:-latest} never executes because curl -f fails the step first

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• Must work for all 7 workflows
  • Must use authenticated GitHub API (with GITHUB_TOKEN) to avoid rate limits
  • Must not require changes to the upstream action
  • Must be a local workaround (composite action or wrapper)
  • Must pin opencode version to avoid the lookup entirely
  • NEVER deploy or touch production
  • NEVER commit secrets

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
1. Fix the rate limit failure so agent jobs can start
  2. Work reliably on shared GitHub runners
  3. Be maintainable (single place to update opencode version)
  4. Preserve all current action inputs (agent, model, prompt, use_github_token, etc.)
  5. Minimal migration effort across 7 workflows

docs.title: Unknowns / Assumptions
docs.text:
• The exact opencode installation method (binary download? npm? script?)
  • Whether the action supports a version input (issue says it doesn't)
  • Current opencode version to pin
  • Whether the action does anything beyond installation (auth setup, config generation)

docs.title: Option A: Local Composite Action (Architect's Proposal)
docs.text:
Create a local composite action .github/actions/opencode-install that reimplements the opencode installation and execution logic using authenticated GitHub API calls, preserving the exact same input interface as the upstream action. Replace all 7 workflow references from uses: anomalyco/opencode/github@latest to uses: ./.github/actions/opencode-install.

Description: - New composite action at .github/actions/opencode-install/action.yml - Pins opencode version in the action (e.g., v0.1.23) - Uses GITHUB_TOKEN for authenticated API calls if version lookup ever needed - Implements robust fallback: pinned version → authenticated latest lookup → error - Mirrors all upstream inputs: agent, model, prompt, use_github_token, etc. - Each workflow changes only the uses: line

Advantages: - Single source of truth for opencode version - Uses authenticated API (avoids 60 req/hr limit) - Preserves all upstream inputs - 7 workflows change only the uses: line — no input restructuring - Composite action runs on runner directly (no container overhead) - Full control over installation logic

Disadvantages: - We own the installation logic (must track upstream changes) - Need to reverse-engineer how opencode is distributed - Slightly more code to maintain than a wrapper

Risks: - If opencode changes release artifact structure, our action breaks - If upstream adds new inputs, we must mirror them - Initial implementation requires discovering actual install method

docs.title: Option B: Pre-step Version Lookup + Pinned Action Reference
docs.text:
Add a preliminary step in each workflow that fetches the version using authenticated curl with GITHUB_TOKEN, then passes it to the upstream action via a version input (if supported) or uses a pinned action reference like anomalyco/opencode/github@v0.1.23.

Description: - Each workflow adds a step: Get opencode version (authenticated) - Uses gh api or authenticated curl with GITHUB_TOKEN - Pins the action to a specific version tag - Only works if upstream action accepts version input or we pin the action ref

Advantages: - Minimal code change (just add step + pin action ref) - No new action to maintain - Authenticated lookup solves rate limit

Disadvantages: - Issue states upstream action has NO version input - Pinning action ref (@v0.1.23) still runs that version's code, which may have the same unauthenticated curl bug - Must update 7 workflows individually when version changes - Doesn't fix the root cause in the action's code

Risks: - If pinned action version has the bug, it still fails - Version drift across 7 workflows - Upstream action may not be semantically versioned

docs.title: Option C: Fork and Fix Upstream Action
docs.text:
Fork anomalyco/opencode repository, fix the unauthenticated curl (add || true fallback or use authenticated API), publish to our own GitHub account, and reference our fork.

Description: - Fork the action repo - Fix the version lookup step - Use uses: our-org/opencode/github@latest (or pinned) - Submit PR upstream

Advantages: - Fixes root cause - Benefits community - Clean separation

Disadvantages: - Requires maintaining a fork - Upstream may not accept PR - Still need to pin version or trust latest on fork - More operational overhead

Risks: - Fork diverges from upstream - Security responsibility for forked action - Delay in getting fixes from upstream

docs.title: Option D: Wrapper Script Action
docs.text:
Create a simple wrapper that installs opencode via a known method (e.g., npm install -g opencode or download from known URL pattern) and then invokes it, bypassing the upstream action entirely.

Description: - Composite action that runs npm install -g @opencode/cli@<pinned-version> or similar - Then runs opencode with the provided arguments - No GitHub API calls at all

Advantages: - Zero GitHub API dependency - Simple, reliable - Version pinned in one place

Disadvantages: - Assumes npm distribution (may not be how opencode is distributed) - May miss action-specific setup (auth, config, environment) - Need to verify opencode CLI interface matches action expectations

Risks: - If opencode isn't on npm, this fails - Action may do more than just npx opencode ...

docs.title: Discussion
docs.text:
The architect's Option A (local composite action) is the only approach that satisfies ALL constraints simultaneously: 1. ✅ Works for all 7 workflows (single uses: change each) 2. ✅ Uses authenticated API (via GITHUB_TOKEN in composite action) 3. ✅ No upstream changes needed 4. ✅ Local workaround 5. ✅ Pins version in one place 6. ✅ Preserves all inputs (drop-in replacement) 7. ✅ Minimal migration (one line per workflow)

Option B fails because the upstream action has no version input and pinning the action ref doesn't fix the buggy code inside that version.

Option C adds operational overhead (maintaining a fork) and doesn't eliminate the need for a local solution if upstream rejects the fix.

Option D is attractive but risky without knowing opencode's distribution method. The composite action in Option A can START with Option D's approach (direct install) and fall back to authenticated GitHub Releases API if needed.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: Selected solution: Option A — Local Composite Action

docs.title: Why
docs.text:
• Only option meeting all hard constraints
  • Single point of version control
  • Drop-in replacement for all 7 workflows
  • Authenticated API access built-in
  • Extensible for future opencode changes
  • Follows GitHub Actions best practice (local actions for customization)

docs.title: Trade-offs
docs.text:
• We own the installation logic (maintenance burden)
  • Must reverse-engineer opencode distribution initially
  • Slight risk if opencode changes distribution method

docs.title: Risks
docs.text:
• Mitigated by: Pinning a known-good version initially; adding automated dependabot-like check for new releases
  • Monitored by: Watching upstream releases; testing in a branch before merging

docs.title: Rejected Alternatives
docs.text:
• Option B: Upstream action has no version input; pinning ref doesn't fix internal bug
  • Option C: Fork maintenance overhead; upstream acceptance uncertain
  • Option D: Unknown distribution method; may miss action-specific setup

1. Investigate opencode distribution method (check upstream action source or releases)
  2. Create .github/actions/opencode-install/action.yml composite action
  3. Test with one workflow (e.g., opencode-pr-review.yml)
  4. Migrate remaining 6 workflows
  5. Add version update automation (optional)

docs.title: Confidence
docs.text: HIGH — The constraints leave only one viable path, and composite actions are a well-established GitHub Actions pattern for exactly this use case.

1. Specification Readiness Assessment

The specification at docs/ai/plans/PLAN-41-household-create.md is complete and implementation-ready. It correctly follows the established patterns in the codebase:

  • ✅ Domain layer follows Expense aggregate pattern (factory create, reconstruct, private constructor, immutability)
  • ✅ Application layer uses ports (HouseholdRepository, extended MemberRepository) with no Spring dependencies
  • ✅ Infrastructure uses Spring Data JPA adapters with mapper pattern (HouseholdMapper, MemberRepositoryImpl)
  • ✅ API layer uses explicit DTOs (CreateHouseholdRequest, CreateHouseholdResponse) — no persistence entities exposed
  • ✅ Household isolation enforced server-side (generated IDs, no client-supplied household ID)
  • ✅ Test strategy covers all layers (domain unit, application mocked, integration, API)
  • ✅ Flyway migration V3 adds role column correctly with data migration for existing rows

docs.title: 2. Technical Risks & Decisions
docs.text: Risk/Decision Assessment Resolution Member role in domain vs. application Spec defines HouseholdMember in domain with role, but Member port record lacks role Correct: role is a domain concern within HouseholdMember entity; application Member record remains lean (used for membership verification only). Adapter maps role at persistence boundary. MemberRepository.save() signature Spec adds save(Member) to port, but Member record has no role Adapter MemberRepositoryImpl.save() accepts Member and persists with role default (MEMBER); use case overrides for OWNER via JPA entity constructor. Acceptable for MVP. Event publication Direct via ApplicationEventPublisher (synchronous) Acceptable for MVP. Outbox pattern can be introduced later via ADR. Email format validation Spec suggests @Email on API DTO only Correct: domain shouldn't know email format rules. API validation suffices. Member ID generation Random UUID in use case Matches existing pattern (Expense uses UUID.randomUUID()). Deterministic IDs not needed without auth. Rollback safety of V3 migration Adds role column with DEFAULT 'MEMBER' and backfills Safe: ALTER TABLE ... ADD COLUMN ... DEFAULT is metadata-only in PG 11+. Backfill UPDATE is idempotent. Rollback = DROP COLUMN role.

package com.sharedhousehold.application.usecase.household;

import com.sharedhousehold.application.command.household.CreateHouseholdCommand;
import com.sharedhousehold.application.command.household.CreateHouseholdResult;
import com.sharedhousehold.application.exception.InvalidHouseholdException;
import com.sharedhousehold.application.port.household.HouseholdRepository;
import com.sharedhousehold.application.port.MemberRepository;
import com.sharedhousehold.domain.household.Household;
import com.sharedhousehold.domain.household.HouseholdId;
import com.sharedhousehold.domain.household.HouseholdMember;
import com.sharedhousehold.domain.household.MemberRole;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Service;
import org.springframework.transaction.annotation.Transactional;
import org.springframework.context.ApplicationEventPublisher;

import java.time.Instant;
import java.util.UUID;

@Service
@Transactional
public class CreateHouseholdUseCase {

    private final HouseholdRepository householdRepository;
    private final MemberRepository memberRepository;
    private final ApplicationEventPublisher eventPublisher;

    public CreateHouseholdUseCase(HouseholdRepository householdRepository,
                                   MemberRepository memberRepository,
                                   ApplicationEventPublisher eventPublisher) {
        this.householdRepository = householdRepository;
        this.memberRepository = memberRepository;
        this.eventPublisher = eventPublisher;
    }

    public CreateHouseholdResult execute(CreateHouseholdCommand command) {
        // 1. Validate creator email uniqueness within household (not needed for new household, but keep for consistency)
        // 2. Create Household aggregate
        HouseholdId householdId = HouseholdId.generate();
        Household household = Household.create(householdId, command.name());

        // 3. Create creator as OWNER member
        UUID creatorMemberId = UUID.randomUUID();
        HouseholdMember ownerMember = HouseholdMember.createOwner(creatorMemberId, householdId);

        // 4. Persist household first
        Household savedHousehold = householdRepository.save(household);

        // 5. Persist creator member
        Member creatorMember = new Member(creatorMemberId, householdId.getValue(), command.creatorName(), command.creatorEmail());
        Member savedMember = memberRepository.save(creatorMember);

        // 6. Publish domain events
        eventPublisher.publishEvent(new HouseholdCreated(householdId, command.name(), creatorMemberId, Instant.now()));
        eventPublisher.publishEvent(new MemberAdded(householdId, creatorMemberId, MemberRole.OWNER, Instant.now()));

        return new CreateHouseholdResult(
                savedHousehold.getId(),
                savedHousehold.getName(),
                savedMember.id(),
                MemberRole.OWNER,
                savedHousehold.getCreatedAt());
    }
}

package com.sharedhousehold.infrastructure.persistence.household;

public class HouseholdRepositoryImpl implements HouseholdRepository {

    private final HouseholdJpaRepository householdJpaRepository;
    private final HouseholdMapper mapper;

    public HouseholdRepositoryImpl(HouseholdJpaRepository householdJpaRepository, HouseholdMapper mapper) {
        this.householdJpaRepository = householdJpaRepository;
        this.mapper = mapper;

    @Override
    public Household save(Household household) {
        HouseholdJpaEntity entity = HouseholdMapper.toJpaEntity(household);
        HouseholdJpaEntity savedEntity = householdJpaRepository.save(entity);
        return HouseholdMapper.toDomain(savedEntity);

    @Override

        return householdJpaRepository.findById(id.getValue())
                .map(HouseholdMapper::toDomain);
    }

    @Override
    public boolean existsById(HouseholdId id) {
        return householdJpaRepository.existsById(id.getValue());
    }
}

package com.sharedhousehold.api.household;

import com.sharedhousehold.application.command.household.CreateHouseholdCommand;
import com.sharedhousehold.application.command.household.CreateHouseholdResult;
import com.sharedhousehold.application.exception.household.InvalidHouseholdException;
import com.sharedhousehold.application.usecase.household.CreateHouseholdUseCase;
import io.swagger.v3.oas.annotations.Operation;
import io.swagger.v3.oas.annotations.media.Content;
import io.swagger.v3.oas.annotations.media.Schema;
import io.swagger.v3.oas.annotations.responses.ApiResponse;
import io.swagger.v3.oas.annotations.responses.ApiResponses;
import io.swagger.v3.oas.annotations.tags.Tag;
import jakarta.validation.Valid;
import org.springframework.http.HttpStatus;
import org.springframework.http.ResponseEntity;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.ExceptionHandler;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.PostMapping;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.RequestBody;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.RequestMapping;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.RestController;

@RestController
@RequestMapping("/api/households")
@Tag(name = "Households", description = "Household management endpoints")
public class HouseholdController {

    private final CreateHouseholdUseCase createHouseholdUseCase;

    public HouseholdController(CreateHouseholdUseCase createHouseholdUseCase) {
        this.createHouseholdUseCase = createHouseholdUseCase;
    }

    @PostMapping
    @Operation(
            summary = "Create a new household",
            description = "Creates a new household with the requester as the owner member")
    @ApiResponses(value = {
            @ApiResponse(
                    responseCode = "201",
                    description = "Household created successfully",
                    content = @Content(schema = @Schema(implementation = CreateHouseholdResponse.class))),
            @ApiResponse(
                    responseCode = "400",
                    description = "Invalid request data",
                    content = @Content(schema = @Schema(implementation = ErrorResponse.class))),
            @ApiResponse(
                    responseCode = "409",
                    description = "Email already in use (future: when auth is added)",
                    content = @Content(schema = @Schema(implementation = ErrorResponse.class)))
    })
    public ResponseEntity<CreateHouseholdResponse> createHousehold(@Valid @RequestBody CreateHouseholdRequest request) {
        CreateHouseholdCommand command = new CreateHouseholdCommand(
                request.name(),
                request.creatorName(),
                request.creatorEmail());

        CreateHouseholdResult result = createHouseholdUseCase.execute(command);
        return ResponseEntity.status(HttpStatus.CREATED).body(toResponse(result));
    }

    @ExceptionHandler(InvalidHouseholdException.class)
    public ResponseEntity<ErrorResponse> handleInvalidHousehold(InvalidHouseholdException e) {
        return ResponseEntity.status(HttpStatus.BAD_REQUEST).body(new ErrorResponse(e.getMessage()));
    }

    @ExceptionHandler(IllegalArgumentException.class)
    public ResponseEntity<ErrorResponse> handleIllegalArgument(IllegalArgumentException e) {
        return ResponseEntity.status(HttpStatus.BAD_REQUEST).body(new ErrorResponse(e.getMessage()));
    }

    private CreateHouseholdResponse toResponse(CreateHouseholdResult result) {
        return new CreateHouseholdResponse(
                result.householdId().getValue(),
                result.name(),
                result.creatorMemberId(),
                result.creatorRole().name(),
                result.createdAt());
    }

    @Schema(description = "Error response")
    public record ErrorResponse(@Schema(description = "Error message") String message) {}
}

docs.title: 10. Open Questions
docs.text:
1. Email uniqueness: Should we enforce unique email per household at DB level? (Current V1 schema has UNIQUE (household_id, email) — this is correct for within-household uniqueness. Cross-household uniqueness requires auth.)

  2. Member ID generation: Should the creator's member ID be deterministic (e.g., derived from email) or random UUID? Random UUID is simpler and matches existing pattern.

  3. Household name uniqueness: Should household names be unique globally? No — different households can have same name.

  4. Event publication: Use Spring's ApplicationEventPublisher (synchronous) or async? Synchronous is fine for MVP; async can be added later.

  5. Creator email validation: Should we validate email format in domain or only in API? API validation (Jakarta @Email) is sufficient; domain doesn't need to know email format rules.

docs.title: Open questions
docs.text:
1. Token storage: Refresh tokens — store hash in DB (revocable) or stateless JWT with short expiry + refresh token rotation? Stateless is simpler for MVP; revocable adds a refresh_tokens table. Recommendation: Start stateless with rotation (issue new refresh token on each refresh, invalidate old).

  2. Email uniqueness: Global (across all households) or per-household? Current members table has UNIQUE (household_id, email). For users table, global unique email makes sense for login.

  3. User ↔ Member linking: When a registered user creates/joins a household, how to link? Option A: User has memberId per household (many-to-many via join table). Option B: Keep separate — Member has optional userId FK. Recommendation: Option B — add nullable user_id to members table in a future migration (not in Phase 0).

  4. Password requirements: Min length, complexity? Enforce at API layer (validation annotations) and/or domain.

  5. Rate limiting: Apply to /api/auth/* endpoints? Defer to follow-up (per security.md abuse considerations).

  6. JWT library: io.jsonwebtoken:jjwt (0.12.x) vs Spring Security's built-in JwtDecoder/JwtEncoder (Spring Security 6+). Recommendation: Use jjwt for token generation/parsing (more control), Spring Security for filter chain integration.

  7. Test profile security: Current tests disable security globally (spring.security.enabled=false). For auth tests, need a separate test slice or profile with security enabled. Approach: Create AuthControllerTest with @ActiveProfiles("auth-test") and separate application-auth-test.properties with security enabled.

docs.title: Modular monolith
docs.text:
The first version is a modular monolith, not microservices. One deployable application with clear module boundaries.

Why not microservices first:

  • The domain (household ledger) has strong consistency requirements; distributed transactions across services would add cost without benefit at this stage.
  • Small team and small product: a monolith has lower operational overhead, simpler local development, and fewer failure modes.
  • The modular boundaries still allow later extraction into services if a module genuinely needs independent scaling or ownership — but that decision must be justified and documented in an ADR.

Containerization/Kubernetes can be introduced later if deployment requirements justify it. Do not over-engineer the MVP.

docs.title: Hexagonal architecture (ports and adapters)
docs.text:
• Domain: pure business logic, no Spring or database dependencies.
  • Application: use cases / application services orchestrate the domain through ports.
  • Infrastructure: adapters implement ports (persistence, HTTP) and wire in Spring and the database.

Rules:

  • Keep business logic out of controllers.
  • Use explicit request/response DTOs.
  • Never expose persistence entities directly as public API contracts.

docs.title: Data
docs.text: PostgreSQL is the transactional source of truth. Schema changes require migrations. See docs/architecture/domain-model.md for the domain model and the database skill for persistence rules.

docs.title: Money
docs.text: Never use floating point for money. Use a domain-level money abstraction and exact decimal arithmetic (such as BigDecimal) with explicit currency. Rounding rules must be defined and tested.

docs.title: Working example
docs.text:
Alice pays €90 for groceries.

Alice share   €30
Bob share     €30
Charlie share €30

Alice paid €90 and owes €30 => +€60 net
Bob owes €30                => -€30 net
Charlie owes €30            => -€30 net

Keep the five concepts distinct: who paid, who participated, who owes, how the amount was allocated, and how a debt was settled.

docs.title: Initial domain invariants
docs.text:
Initial rules — subject to explicit refinement, never silently changed:

  1. An expense belongs to exactly one household.
  2. The payer must be a member of the household.
  3. Participants must be members of the same household.
  4. Allocations cannot be negative.
  5. Total allocation must equal the expense total, subject to a deterministic rounding policy.
  6. Currency must be explicit.
  7. Financial calculations must be deterministic.
  8. A member must not access another household's private financial data merely by changing an identifier in a request.
  9. Settlement is separate from the original expense.
  10. Editing an expense must preserve a clear audit/history strategy once that functionality is implemented.

docs.title: Security
docs.text: Detailed authentication provider decisions are intentionally deferred. This document records the security rules and review lenses now; concrete provider choices (identity provider, token strategy) are separate decisions to be made with a human when authentication baseline work begins.

docs.title: Authentication
docs.text:
• Who the user is. Scope: login/registration as a roadmap item (Phase 0).
  • Provider and token strategy are deferred decisions.

docs.title: Authorization
docs.text:
• Who can do what inside a household.
  • Authorization is separate from authentication and must be handled explicitly.

docs.title: Household isolation
docs.text:
• Mandatory. A member must not access another household's expenses, members, balances, settlements, or products by changing an identifier in a request (IDOR).
  • Every household-scoped read/write must verify membership before acting.
  • Never trust household identifiers coming from clients without authorization checks.

docs.title: Input validation
docs.text:
• Validate all inputs at the boundary: unexpected shapes, invalid identifiers, impossible amounts.
  • Validation errors must be meaningful and must not leak internals.

docs.title: Secret handling
docs.text:
• Secrets must never be committed to the repository.
  • Credentials stay outside repository files and out of logs.

docs.title: Auditability
docs.text:
• Financial operations should be auditable.
  • Editing expenses must preserve an audit/history strategy once implemented.

docs.title: Abuse / rate-limit considerations
docs.text:
• Public endpoints (e.g. invitation acceptance, expense creation) should consider rate limits and abuse controls.
  • These are design considerations for baseline work, not implemented yet.

docs.title: Review lens (for the security-reviewer agent)
docs.text: Authentication, authorization, household/member isolation, IDOR/access-control issues, input validation, injection, secrets, sensitive data exposure, insecure deserialization, dependency vulnerabilities, API abuse, tenant isolation.

docs.title: Trust boundaries
docs.text:
Browser (untrusted)
  -> REST API (authentication + authorization at the boundary)
  -> Domain/application layer (enforces invariants)
  -> PostgreSQL (transactional source of truth)

docs.title: Status
docs.text: Accepted

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
Baseline code review (issue #2) found two security findings in the OpenCode agent configuration: - C1: qa-engineer has unrestricted bash: allow — the most dangerous permission, inconsistent with all other agents. - C2: backend-implementer and frontend-implementer have NO permission: block at all — the two write-capable agents are least constrained.

This violates the least-privilege principle and the repository's security rules (AGENTS.md: "Never give database write access to unknown/untrusted clients", "Household isolation is mandatory").

Reference: Brainstorming report BR-001, GitHub Issue #5.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: Apply restrictive, consistent permission blocks to all three agents following the established orchestrator/code-reviewer/security-reviewer pattern (map form with allowlist + "*": deny fallback).

docs.title: qa-engineer
docs.text:
• edit: deny, write: deny
  • read: allow, glob: allow, grep: allow, list: allow
  • bash: { "mvn *": allow, "npm *": allow, "*": deny }
  • Explicit denies: webfetch, websearch, task, skill, external_directory

docs.title: backend-implementer
docs.text:
• read: allow, glob: allow, grep: allow, list: allow
  • edit/write: { "src/**": allow, "pom.xml": allow, ".opencode/**": deny, "docs/architecture/security.md": deny, "*": deny }
  • bash: { "mvn *": allow, "*": deny }
  • Explicit denies: webfetch, websearch, task, skill, external_directory

docs.title: frontend-implementer
docs.text:
• read: allow, glob: allow, grep: allow, list: allow
  • edit/write: { "frontend/**": allow, ".opencode/**": deny, "docs/architecture/security.md": deny, "*": deny }
  • bash: { "npm *": allow, "npx *": allow, "*": deny }
  • Explicit denies: webfetch, websearch, task, skill, external_directory

docs.title: Alternatives Considered
docs.text:
1. Broad permissive (edit: allow, write: allow) — rejected: violates least privilege, inconsistent, security risk.
  2. Narrow path scoping (src/main/java/** only) — rejected: too restrictive, breaks legitimate work (resources, test fixtures).
  3. File-type patterns (**/*.java) — rejected: misses non-standard extensions; directory patterns more maintainable.
  4. Test-only bash for QA (mvn test*) — rejected: too restrictive; QA needs clean, dependency:tree, etc.
  5. Omitting explicit tool denies — rejected: implicit deny per schema, but explicit is clearer for audit.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
Positive: - All agents now follow consistent least-privilege pattern - C1 and C2 findings resolved - Defense-in-depth via sensitive path denies (.opencode/**, docs/architecture/security.md) - Explicit audit trail for all tools

Negative: - More verbose permission blocks - Sensitive path deny list requires maintenance - Edge-case file paths (Docker, scripts) may need future allowlist extensions

docs.title: Addendum (2026-09-22, GitHub-native operation)
docs.text:
To let agents operate inside GitHub Actions runners (the GitHub-native workflow), the bash allowlists were extended with git/gh commands:

  • backend-implementer / frontend-implementer: added "git *": allow and "gh *": allow (needed to commit, branch, push, open/update PRs). Existing edit/write path scoping and sensitive-path denies are unchanged.
  • qa-engineer: added "git *": allow and "gh *": allow (diff/evidence reporting). QA remains edit: deny — it never modifies production files.
  • orchestrator: edit/write narrowed to docs/** + AGENTS.md (reports, decisions); bash allows git * and gh * for state reconstruction and recovery reporting; task: allow (delegation) retained; websearch/ webfetch set to ask.

This is a controlled broadening for GitHub-native execution. It does not relax the human gate: write-capable implementer access in CI additionally requires the trusted-actor rule (repository variable OC_TRUSTED_ACTORS) and per-workflow job permissions; QA and reviewers remain non-writers. The original restriction was relaxed explicitly so the change is auditable rather than silent.

docs.title: Revisit Triggers
docs.text:
• If backend-implementer legitimately needs to edit files outside src/** and pom.xml (e.g., Docker, CI scripts)
  • If QA needs non-Maven/npm commands (docker, psql for test DB)
  • If new tools are added to the permission schema that these agents might need
  • If the agent roster changes significantly (new agents added)

docs.title: Addendum: project-manager (2026-09-26)
docs.text:
Triggered by the roster-change revisit trigger above, following ADR-002.

project-manager is added with an explicit restrictive permission: block, following the same map-form pattern as this ADR rather than the wildcard form that caused findings C1/C2:

Capability Setting Rationale read, grep, glob, list allow Reconciliation is read-mostly. edit / write docs/**, AGENTS.md only; *: deny The manager may maintain docs/product/roadmap.md execution status and its own policy docs. It must never edit application source. bash git *, gh * only; *: deny Sufficient for issue/label/PR/CI/ledger operations and workflow dispatch. It is not given mvn, npm, docker or any database client, so it cannot build, test or touch a database itself — it delegates execution and reads evidence instead. task allow This is how it delegates to specialists. webfetch, websearch ask Same posture as the orchestrator. external_directory deny Unchanged. Writes outside the repository hang CI.

Two consequences of this block worth recording explicitly:

  • The manager is not able to run the test suite. This is intentional. It must not be able to make a build pass; it reads CI and QA results as evidence. Giving it mvn would have let it self-certify its own merge gates.
  • gh * is broad enough to include gh pr merge, which the manager is permitted to use under the gate policy in ADR-002. Least privilege is therefore enforced at the prompt-contract and test layer for that one operation, not by the permission schema, which cannot express it. The prohibitions (--admin, guardrail merges, bypassing branch protection) are pinned by scripts/test-project-manager.sh.

No existing agent's permissions were widened or narrowed by this change.

docs.title: Status
docs.text: Accepted

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
The agent suite had a well-defined delivery pipeline but no owner of product-level state. The orchestrator coordinates one bounded execution (analyze → implement → QA → review) for a single issue. Nothing in the system:

  • decided what the next piece of work should be;
  • noticed that the roadmap had moved past what the issues described;
  • noticed a PR had been sitting in review for three days, or that an agent had failed and left an issue stranded with no owner;
  • created follow-up work when an implementation PR revealed a missing prerequisite;
  • distinguished "an agent said done" from "the feature is verifiably complete";
  • kept a durable record of why a piece of work exists and what it unblocks.

This was already causing observable drift. docs/product/roadmap.md carried no execution status at all, so the intended sequence existed only as prose, and the autonomy pipeline had begun producing stacked PRs on agent branches with no component reasoning about dependency order.

A top-level manager was requested to close that gap, with the founder retaining product vision and remaining the safety boundary.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
1. Add project-manager (.opencode/agents/project-manager.md), the Autonomous Product & Engineering Manager, positioned above the orchestrator. It owns delivery state, sequencing, and progress. It does not own product vision and it does not implement code.

  2. GitHub remains the only durable state. The manager reconstructs project state from issues, PRs, labels, CI, ADRs and repository documents on every cycle. Durable manager bookkeeping (run log, budget counters, retry attempts) lives in a single pinned Manager Ledger issue, precisely so that no state exists only in model context.

  3. GitHub labels are authoritative for actual work state. docs/product/roadmap.md gains an execution-status column that the manager mirrors; if the two disagree, labels win.

  4. Autonomy is a separate dial. A new MANAGER_AUTONOMY repository variable (human_only | supervised | autonomous, default supervised) governs the manager, deliberately independent of the existing AUTOPILOT switch. The manager's power can therefore be raised or lowered without changing how the existing pipeline behaves, and the manager cannot gain authority merely because AUTOPILOT happens to be on.

  5. Event-driven execution plus a scheduled heartbeat, not a long-running process. GitHub Actions remains the only runtime.

  6. Risk classes (LOW/MEDIUM/HIGH/CRITICAL) determine which gates apply. CRITICAL is propose-only, always. Money, currency, rounding, allocations, balances and settlements are HIGH or above by default, and financial validation may never be weakened to make work pass.

  7. Bounded, budgeted action. Per-cycle issue caps, PR-in-flight caps and bounded retries, so the loop degrades gracefully instead of running away. A pause/emergency-stop path exists and must be able to start no new work.

docs.title: The merge decision, recorded as an explicit override
docs.text:
The recommended design was that the manager never merges and instead delegates merging to the existing pipeline's auto-merge step, which already enforces the QA/review/guardrail gates. The owner reviewed this and chose the opposite: the manager merges implementation PRs directly after evaluating the gates.

Concretely, the manager runs an ordinary gh pr merge --squash under normal branch protection, as the same automation identity. That ordinaryness is the point: there is no privileged merge path, so branch protection has the final say in every case.

This is recorded here because it is the highest-risk element of the design and it was a deliberate choice against advice. The known costs:

  • A second merge path now exists. Every gate the pipeline enforces must be re-implemented correctly in the manager, and the two can drift apart.
  • The manager runs under the same GitHub identity (GITHUB_TOKEN) as the agents that author the PRs it would merge, so GitHub branch protection may refuse the merge. That refusal is a fail-safe and must be respected.
  • A bug in the manager's gate evaluation becomes an ungated merge, which is strictly worse than a missing merge.

Compensating controls, all mandatory:

  • The manager must never use --admin, never bypass branch protection, and never force-push main. If protection blocks it, it stops and escalates.
  • Guardrail changes are never merged by the manager. Any PR touching .github/, .opencode/, AGENTS.md or oc-models.json goes to the founder, by hand, always. This preserves the existing guardrail exemption and stops the suite from rewriting its own constraints.
  • CRITICAL-risk changes are propose-only and never merged.
  • The gate list is pinned by an executable test (scripts/test-project-manager.sh) that fails if a required gate string or prohibition is removed from the agent contract, and is mutation-checked to prove it can actually fail.
  • The founder can reduce the manager to supervised (stop before merge) or human_only at any time with a single variable, without a code change.

If the second merge path is ever observed to be a problem in practice, the fallback is to revert decision 7's merge clause to delegation; the rest of the manager is unaffected.

docs.title: Alternatives considered
docs.text:
1. Extend the existing orchestrator instead of adding an agent. Rejected: the orchestrator's contract is explicitly scoped to one bounded task, runs as mode: primary, and is forbidden from merging. Widening it would change the behaviour of every existing pipeline phase.

  2. A separate external scheduler / long-running worker process. Rejected: introduces a new runtime, a new credential surface and a process that must be operated. GitHub Actions already provides event triggers, cron and concurrency groups, and OpenCode already runs inside it.

  3. Keep a JSON/YAML backlog file in the repository as manager state. Rejected: it becomes a second source of truth that drifts from GitHub and invites write conflicts from concurrent agents. A pinned issue is atomic, auditable, human-editable and already covered by the label state machine.

  4. A GitHub Project as the authoritative dashboard. Rejected for now: the repository has no Project configuration and no token with project-write scope, so automated field management cannot work without a new secret. Labels are already an adequate state store; the Project stays a manual view.

  5. Manager merges nothing (recommended, not chosen). Recorded above with its costs and the fallback path.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
Positive

  • The project has an owner for sequencing, dependency order and stalled work.
  • "Next value" becomes a decision with a documented reason rather than an accident of who filed an issue.
  • Completion is evidence-based, not self-reported.
  • Autonomy, risk, budget and emergency stop become explicit, inspectable and reversible configuration instead of emergent behaviour.
  • The manager is inert until explicitly enabled, so adopting it is reversible.

Negative / accepted

  • More moving parts, and a larger guardrail surface to review.
  • A second merge path (see above).
  • Proactive issue creation can still generate noise; bounded by the per-cycle cap and the "never create work to look busy" rule, and both are enforced by prompt contract and tests rather than by code.
  • The manager is a reasoning model and can be wrong about state. Mitigated by requiring evidence, and by status:blocked being an acceptable outcome.

docs.title: Revisit Triggers
docs.text:
• Any observed ungated merge, or a merge attempted with --admin.
  • Branch protection refusing a legitimate manager merge, which would mean the same-identity problem needs a distinct GitHub App identity.
  • The per-cycle issue cap being hit routinely, which would mean the budget is mis-tuned rather than the manager being over-eager.
  • Drift between the manager's merge gates and the pipeline's auto-merge gates.
  • A request to make the Project authoritative, which would require adding a project-write credential.

docs.title: Agent protocol
docs.text: AI agents have bounded roles. The roles below are realized by the agents defined in .opencode/agents/; this document defines the contract each role obeys. See docs/ai/agent-strategy.md for how the roles are sequenced and docs/ai/model-strategy.md for model assignments.

docs.title: Orchestrator
docs.text:
Responsibilities:

  • read the issue
  • decide whether a design decision exists
  • decide whether specification is needed
  • select the minimum required specialist agents
  • launch collaborative brainstorming when a design decision exists
  • pass only relevant context
  • stop unnecessary agent chains
  • summarize state after every major phase

Must not:

  • implement directly
  • edit or write files
  • invent requirements

docs.title: Brainstormer
docs.text:
Responsibilities:

  • orchestrate a structured discussion (problem framing, independent proposals, cross-critique, synthesis) among only the relevant specialists
  • select a solution autonomously per the decision policy
  • write a durable brainstorming report to docs/ai/brainstorms/
  • create or update an ADR when the decision has long-term consequences

Must not:

  • act as a single-answer agent
  • implement production code
  • modify anything outside docs/
  • stop and ask the user merely because several solutions exist

Blocking is allowed only for genuinely unsafe, impossible, or contradictory tasks, and always produces a BLOCKED report.

docs.title: Product/planning agent
docs.text:
Responsibilities:

  • inspect the issue
  • inspect relevant product docs
  • identify missing business rules
  • produce implementation-ready requirements
  • call out ambiguity explicitly

Must not:

  • write production code
  • redesign the product
  • invent requirements silently

docs.title: Architect
docs.text:
Responsibilities:

  • inspect the existing architecture
  • identify affected modules, domain changes, persistence changes, API changes, migrations, and testing strategy
  • produce a compact implementation plan

Must not:

  • edit files
  • rewrite unrelated parts of the application

docs.title: Implementation agent (backend / frontend)
docs.text:
Responsibilities:

  • implement an approved task
  • follow the architecture
  • write tests
  • update required documentation
  • run verification (focused first, broader when useful)

Must not:

  • change unrelated features
  • redesign the architecture without an ADR or explicit request
  • alter product scope silently
  • claim tests passed without running them

docs.title: QA agent
docs.text:
Responsibilities:

  • map acceptance criteria to tests/evidence
  • identify missing scenarios
  • inspect edge cases
  • run relevant tests
  • report PASS / FAIL / BLOCKED per criterion

Must not:

  • redefine acceptance criteria without stating the discrepancy
  • modify production code
  • claim PASS without evidence

docs.title: Code reviewer
docs.text:
Responsibilities:

  • inspect the diff
  • look for correctness problems
  • detect regressions
  • inspect architecture violations
  • identify missing tests
  • report findings by severity

Must not:

  • modify production code
  • rewrite the implementation

docs.title: Security reviewer
docs.text:
Responsibilities:

  • inspect security boundaries and tenant/household isolation
  • verify that a user cannot access another household's data by changing an identifier
  • check authentication, authorization, input validation, secrets, and abuse controls

Must not:

  • modify production code

docs.title: Documentation agent
docs.text:
Responsibilities:

  • update only the documentation needed by a task
  • prefer concise edits

Must not:

  • modify production code or configuration

docs.title: Researcher
docs.text:
Responsibilities:

  • perform external/technical research
  • return cited findings

Must not:

  • edit files
  • broaden the question into open-ended exploration

docs.title: Definition of Done
docs.text:
[ ] acceptance criteria verified
[ ] business rules covered by tests
[ ] implementation follows architecture
[ ] no unrelated changes
[ ] database migration included when required
[ ] API documentation updated when required
[ ] security implications reviewed
[ ] focused tests passed
[ ] broader tests passed when applicable
[ ] code review completed
[ ] issue linked to PR
[ ] documentation updated where necessary
[ ] ready for deployment/acceptance

Never claim a checklist item passed unless it was actually performed.

docs.title: Definition of Ready
docs.text:
An issue may enter READY only if:

[ ] user story exists
[ ] problem/context is clear
[ ] business rules are explicit
[ ] acceptance criteria are testable
[ ] edge cases are identified
[ ] non-goals are identified
[ ] technical constraints are known
[ ] dependencies are identified
[ ] expected test scope is known
[ ] task is small enough to implement safely

If the issue is ambiguous, it belongs in DISCOVERY.

An XL implementation task should normally be decomposed before entering READY.

docs.title: Publishing the documentation site
docs.text: Documentation and agent reports are rendered to a public GitHub Pages site, hosted in the dedicated public repository share-org/share-docs (https://share-org.github.io/share-docs/). The private share repository remains the single source of truth: editing docs/ there republishes the site.

docs.title: The prototype is published too
docs.text:
docs/product/maquette/mockups/app.html is a static file inside docs/, so MkDocs copies it verbatim to https://share-org.github.io/share-docs/product/maquette/mockups/app.html. That is the live prototype: the same file the repository holds, reachable from a browser.

It carries the annotation layer — open it with ?annotate=1, click a component, and it opens a pre-filled issue in share-org/share labeled prototype-feedback. There is no backend and no third-party review service; the annotation layer is plain client-side JavaScript in that one file. Editing the maquette on main republishes it with the rest of the site.

Consequence: the prototype is world-readable, exactly like everything else under docs/. Do not put real household data in the maquette.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
The docs-publish workflow in share (.github/workflows/docs-publish.yml):

  1. Triggers on pushes to main touching docs/** or mkdocs.yml, and on manual workflow_dispatch.
  2. Builds the MkDocs Material site from docs/ (config: mkdocs.yml).
  3. Pushes the built site to the gh-pages branch of the public share-org/share-docs repository, which GitHub Pages serves.

The GitHub Pages site in share-docs is configured to deploy from the gh-pages branch (root). GitHub Pages on the free plan requires the target repository to be public, which is why share-docs is a public repo containing only rendered static content — source code stays private.

docs.title: One-time setup
docs.text:
1. Create a fine-grained personal access token scoped to the share-docs repository only:
  2. GitHub → Settings → Developer settings → Fine-grained tokens → Generate new token.
  3. Repository access: Only select repositories → share-org/share-docs.
  4. Permissions: Contents → Read and write.
  5. Add it as a repository secret in share named SHARE_DOCS_TOKEN (Settings → Secrets and variables → Actions → New repository secret).

Until the secret exists, the publish step is skipped with a warning and the site keeps its previous content.

docs.title: Triggering a republish
docs.text:
• Automatic: any change to docs/** or mkdocs.yml on main.
  • Manual: Actions → docs-publish → Run workflow.

docs.title: Privacy note
docs.text: Anything under docs/ becomes world-readable once published. Keep internal notes (secrets, personal data, credentials) out of docs/.

docs.title: Example Feature: Split an expense by shares
docs.text: This is an example only. Do not implement it.

docs.title: Context
docs.text: A household may want to divide an expense proportionally without manually calculating percentages.

docs.title: User story
docs.text: As a household member, I want to split an expense by shares, so that members can contribute proportionally.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
Alice pays €100.

Alice = 2 shares Bob = 1 share Charlie = 1 share

Total shares = 4

Alice = €50 Bob = €25 Charlie = €25

docs.title: Acceptance criteria
docs.text:
• [ ] user can select shares split
  • [ ] every participant has a positive number of shares
  • [ ] total allocation equals expense total
  • [ ] rounding is deterministic
  • [ ] invalid share counts are rejected

docs.title: Non-goals
docs.text:
• recurring expenses
  • notifications
  • payment provider integration

docs.title: Tests
docs.text:
• 100 / 2,1,1
  • uneven amount / uneven shares
  • zero shares
  • negative shares
  • rounding remainder

docs.title: Lifecycle
docs.text:
IDEA
  -> DISCOVERY
  -> READY
  -> ARCHITECTURE PLAN
  -> IMPLEMENTATION
  -> AUTOMATED VERIFICATION
  -> AI REVIEW
  -> HUMAN REVIEW
  -> MERGE
  -> DEPLOY
  -> ACCEPTANCE
  -> DONE

The central principle:

A coding agent receives a bounded engineering contract, not an open-ended feature request.

Every implementation task defines:

WHO?
WHAT?
WHY?
BUSINESS RULES?
ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA?
EDGE CASES?
NON-GOALS?
TEST EXPECTATIONS?
TECHNICAL CONSTRAINTS?

An issue may enter READY only if it satisfies the docs/development/definition-of-ready.md checklist; otherwise it belongs in DISCOVERY. Completed work must satisfy docs/development/definition-of-done.md.

The ARCHITECTURE PLAN step includes collaborative brainstorming when the task involves a design decision. The orchestrator detects this and delegates to the brainstormer, which selects a solution autonomously and writes a report to docs/ai/brainstorms/ (and an ADR where justified). See docs/ai/agent-strategy.md.

docs.title: Branch rule
docs.text:
One issue should normally map to one branch.

feature/EXP-105-expense-custom-split
fix/EXP-212-rounding-error
chore/OPS-010-ci-baseline

docs.title: Pull request rule
docs.text:
A PR should:

  • reference one primary issue (Closes #123)
  • stay focused (no unrelated changes)
  • include tests
  • include a migration if needed
  • explain externally observable behavior
  • identify AI-agent involvement
  • pass CI before merge

docs.title: Human gate
docs.text:
AI must not be the final approver of a sensitive change. At minimum, human review is required for:

  • authentication/authorization
  • financial calculation changes
  • database destructive migrations
  • external integrations
  • production deployment changes
  • security-sensitive configuration
  • large architecture changes

Implementation and review agents never merge production code automatically. Agent-generated changes must be auditable (AI involvement recorded in the PR).

docs.title: Done Criteria
docs.text:
What "the product is done" means at the product level, as distinct from "this task is done".

The Project Manager tracks completion at five levels and must not conflate them:

task done      -> this issue's acceptance criteria are met
feature done   -> the capability works end to end for a user
milestone done -> every capability in the milestone is done
MVP done       -> every MVP capability below is done
product done   -> every criterion in this document is satisfied

A finished task is not a finished product. The most common failure mode of an autonomous delivery loop is concluding "done" because the queue emptied, or because a large issue merged. Neither means the roadmap advanced.

docs.title: Product-level completion criteria
docs.text: The product is done when all of the following hold. Each is binary and independently checkable.

docs.title: 1. The MVP chain works end to end
docs.text:
Every link in the chain from docs/product/mvp.md works, in order, for a real household with real data:

Authentication -> Household -> Invite members -> Create expense
-> Choose participants -> Split expense -> Calculate balances -> Settle debts

Not "the endpoint exists" — the flow completes, and the data is correct afterwards.

docs.title: 2. The financial core is exact
docs.text:
• Money uses exact decimal arithmetic. No double, no float.
  • Currency is explicit everywhere, never inferred silently.
  • Rounding rules are defined, documented, and covered by tests that assert specific values.
  • Splits sum exactly to the expense total. No lost or invented minor units. Remainder distribution is deterministic.
  • Balances derive from expenses and are consistent with them.
  • Settlements reflect settled amounts correctly and do not double-count.

This is non-negotiable and is treated as HIGH risk throughout. A rounding error that is "close enough" fails this criterion.

docs.title: 3. Household isolation holds
docs.text:
• A member cannot read or write another household's data by changing an identifier in a request.
  • Isolation is enforced server-side, not only in the UI.
  • The rule is covered by tests that attempt the cross-household access and assert refusal.

docs.title: 4. Authentication and authorization are real
docs.text:
• Authentication is implemented and enforced.
  • Authentication and authorization are separate concerns, both present.
  • Secrets are never committed, logged, or exposed to clients.

docs.title: 5. Quality gates are green
docs.text:
• ci is green on main.
  • Every feature has tests: unit for domain logic, integration for persistence, API tests for important endpoints.
  • No skipped, deleted, or tolerated test exists in the financial paths.
  • Code review and security review have passed for the security- and money-sensitive changes.

docs.title: 6. The product is usable
docs.text:
• The published prototype's core flows correspond to implemented behaviour, and prototype feedback has been resolved or explicitly deferred with a reason.
  • UX validation has passed for user-facing work.
  • Required documentation is current: docs/product/, docs/architecture/.

docs.title: 7. The delivery system is itself trustworthy
docs.text:
• The agent workflow, autonomy policy and budget are documented and enforced.
  • No work item is stranded: every open issue has an owner and a next action.
  • No duplicate work exists between open and recently closed issues.

docs.title: 8. Nothing is quietly deferred
docs.text: Anything not done is written down, with a reason. Silent scope reduction is a failure of this criterion — an honest deferral is acceptable, a hidden one is not.

docs.title: How the Project Manager uses this
docs.text:
The manager must not mark the project done while any criterion above is unmet, and must not treat "the backlog is empty" as evidence. When it believes the product is approaching done, it should:

  1. check each criterion explicitly against evidence, not assertion
  2. report which criteria are met, and which are not
  3. for unmet criteria, create or update the work that closes them
  4. leave the final call to the founder — declaring the product done is a product decision, not a delivery one

docs.title: Explicitly not criteria
docs.text:
These do not count toward done, however complete they are:

  • number of merged PRs
  • number of closed issues
  • a green build with no tests
  • documentation volume
  • a working demo that does not persist correct data
  • the absence of open issues

docs.title: Architecture stance
docs.text: The project starts as a modular monolith application, not a distributed microservice system. See docs/architecture/architecture.md.

docs.title: Relationship to the roadmap
docs.text: This MVP is Phase 0 through the expense/balance/settlement part of Phase 3 in docs/product/roadmap.md. Later roadmap phases are hypotheses, not commitments.

docs.title: Personas
docs.text: Personas describe real problems, not demographics. They shape priorities and acceptance criteria.

docs.title: Roommates
docs.text:
Problem: splitting rent, utilities, internet, and shared groceries every month, tracking who paid, and reconciling who owes whom. Manual tables drift and cause conflict when amounts are not equal or someone paid for more than their share.

What they need: a clear record of every shared expense, an explicit split, current balances, and a way to settle up without arguing about the past.

docs.title: Couples / families
docs.text:
Problem: combining household costs (food, household goods, subscriptions, children's expenses) while keeping contributions fair and transparent. One person often ends up as the de-facto accountant.

What they need: a shared ledger they both trust, simple custom splits, and an auditable history that reduces friction and "who owes what" conversations.

docs.title: Friends sharing temporary accommodation
docs.text:
Problem: short-lived sharing (holidays, temporary stays, project housing) where expenses are unequal, commitments are short, and nobody wants to set up heavy financial tooling.

What they need: fast setup, clear one-time splits, quick settlement, and low effort to leave the group cleanly when the arrangement ends.

docs.title: Note
docs.text: These personas are initial and deliberately small. New personas may be added as the product grows, but persona changes are product decisions, not engineering decisions.

docs.title: Product vision
docs.text: Make shared household finances transparent, fair, and easy to reconcile without requiring spreadsheets, manual calculations, or constant messages between household members.

docs.title: Core user problem
docs.text: People sharing a household (roommates, families, friends) split bills, buy shared goods, and track who owes whom. Today this is done in spreadsheets, chat messages, and mental arithmetic. Balances go stale, disputes arise over who paid what or how an amount was split, and settling debts is awkward.

docs.title: Target users
docs.text:
• Roommates sharing rent, utilities, and groceries
  • Couples and families managing shared household finances
  • Friends sharing temporary accommodation or joint trips

See docs/product/personas.md for details.

docs.title: Initial value proposition
docs.text: A transparent household ledger where every expense records who paid, who participated, how the amount was allocated, and how debts are settled. Any member can see the state and trust the numbers, because the rules are explicit and the calculations are deterministic.

docs.title: Long-term direction
docs.text:
The system is intentionally a household ledger and allocation system, not just an expense-splitting calculator. Future concepts (recurring expenses, shared products, shopping lists) build on the same core model.

Future phases documented in docs/product/roadmap.md are hypotheses, not commitments. They are pursued only when the current phase is stable and the need is real.

docs.title: Non-goals (for now)
docs.text: Bank integration, payment providers, OCR, AI assistants, cryptocurrency, taxes, multi-currency conversion, marketplaces, and microservices are all out of scope for the MVP. See docs/product/mvp.md.

docs.title: SharedHousehold — Product maquette
docs.text: Live prototype (GitHub Pages): https://share-org.github.io/share-docs/product/maquette/mockups/app.html — append ?annotate=1 to review a screen and file feedback by clicking. Source of truth: docs/product/maquette/mockups/app.html (open it directly in any browser, nothing to install). Wireframes below. Designer agent: designer. Issue reference: none yet — this is the first design deliverable.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
Show the owner and the implementers what the SharedHousehold app should look and feel like, mapped to the domain in AGENTS.md:

  • who paid
  • who participated
  • who owes
  • how the amount was allocated
  • how a debt was settled

The mockup is data-only (no backend). Every number is deterministic and explicit, because the app is a household ledger, not a splitter.

docs.title: Design principles
docs.text:
1. Calm & trustworthy — money feels safe: soft green accent, generous whitespace, tabular numerals, no alarmist UI.
  2. Explicit allocation — every expense shows who paid, who participated, and the split rule, never hidden inside a "total".
  3. Mobile-first — the living room couch is the primary surface; desktop only adapts the same screens.
  4. Zero-friction settle-up — balances are always visible and once-a-screen settlement suggested, because that's the reason people come back.
  5. Offline-first visuals — no external fonts, CDNs, or icons; the mockup opens from the repo and works forever.

docs.title: How to use
docs.text:
1. Open mockups/app.html in a browser, or the live prototype on GitHub Pages.

  3. Send feedback as a GitHub issue titled with the screen name; the autonomy pipeline picks it up, or a designer agent iterates the maquette.

docs.title: Prototype feedback loop
docs.text:
The maquette ships with an annotation layer: turn it on with ?annotate=1 (or the floating Annotate button), click any component, describe what it should do, and press Open GitHub issue. That opens a pre-filled issue in share-org/share labeled prototype-feedback, carrying the screen, the component's stable data-uid, a CSS-ish path, the prototype URL, and the viewport — so the agents know exactly what was clicked without any screenshot.

Everything is client-side: no backend, no third-party review service, no dependencies. docs-publish.yml publishes the file to the same Pages site as the documentation, so the prototype always matches the code in the repository.

maquette (?annotate=1)  ->  click component  ->  Issue labeled prototype-feedback
   ->  opencode-prototype-feedback.yml
        ->  brainstorm panel: designer (UX), product, architect, backend, QA
        ->  synthesis: BR report + one plan per track
        ->  sub-issues: UX / FRONTEND / BACKEND   (feedback:child-of-<issue>)
   ->  opencode-pipeline.yml, one parallel chain per sub-issue
   ->  parent feedback issue closes when every child is merged
Step Owner Detail Click a component human pre-filled issue, label prototype-feedback Intake brainstormer panel designer, product-planner, architect, backend-implementer, qa-engineer Decision brainstormer docs/ai/brainstorms/BR-NNN-*.md (+ ADR when durable) Decomposition orchestrator one sub-issue + one PLAN-*.md per affected track Execution per sub-issue opencode-pipeline.yml: implement → qa → review → auto-merge Completion pipeline parent closes once no feedback:child-of-<parent> issue is open

Notes:

  • The prototype is a public page, so only issues authored by an account in OC_TRUSTED_ACTORS are picked up automatically. Feedback from anyone else is parked as status:backlog and waits for /oc brainstorm or /oc implement from a trusted human — nothing is discarded.
  • A visual nit (a label, a colour, a copy tweak) is a UX sub-issue only; the intake is instructed to skip the panel and close the parent directly when the feedback needs no design decision.
  • Annotatable elements carry a stable data-uid (dashboard/add-expense-cta, add-expense/split, balances/confirm-settlement, …). Untagged elements are still clickable and are reported as a CSS path. Copy manifest in the panel dumps every annotatable element as JSON.
  • Adding a screen means adding a data-uid to its structural elements — that is what makes the next round of feedback addressable.

See docs/ai/agent-workflow.md for the labels and the pipeline phases.
